sections.title: Emergency systems — the life-safety tier
sections.plain_explanation: Article 700 covers backup power that the law classes as emergency: power for getting people out and keeping them alive, such as egress lighting, exit signs, fire alarm and similar life-safety loads. A governmental agency having jurisdiction decides that a system is emergency; the owner does not get to choose the label. Emergency power has to be there fast — available within 10 seconds of the normal supply failing (700.12) — the wiring is kept completely apart from normal wiring, and the system is tested and documented. If life safety does not depend on it, you are probably in Article 701 or 702 instead.
sections.on_the_job: A single-story daycare in Ocala: the fire marshal requires the egress lighting, exit signs and fire alarm to stay up on generator power, so those loads are Article 700 work before anyone picks gear. Sharma's scope: a Siemens emergency panel fed through listed transfer equipment, the generator carrying the emergency load within 10 seconds, emergency raceways marked as emergency at intervals of 25 ft or less, and no normal-power conductors in the same raceways. The same generator also backs the kitchen refrigerator — that part is Article 702, wired separately, and it never lands on the emergency panel.

sections.why_it_exists: When a building is full of people and the normal power dies, the emergency system is what lights the way out and keeps the alarm talking. If it starts late, shares a raceway that a fault takes out, or was never tested, the failure shows up at the worst possible moment. Article 700 is strict because the loads are not conveniences — they are the evacuation itself.
inspection_fails: Emergency and normal conductors sharing a raceway outside the transfer equipment — emergency wiring stays independent (700.10).

Optional loads — receptacles, comfort HVAC — landed on the emergency panel because there was space.
No written test record: the emergency system was never proven under load, and nothing is documented.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that the owner, the GC, or the size of the generator decides a system is 'emergency.' It does not. A governmental agency having jurisdiction applies the Article 700 label; a big generator feeding a homeowner's refrigerator is still Article 702. Second trap: landing an optional load on the emergency panel 'because there was space' — emergency branch circuits carry emergency loads only.

sections.title: Tests and maintenance — emergency systems
sections.plain_explanation:
An emergency system is not finished when it is wired. 700.3 builds testing and maintenance into the installation itself:
• (A) Acceptance testing: the AHJ conducts or witnesses a test of the complete system when the installation is finished, and periodically afterward.
• (B) Periodic testing: the system is tested periodically on a schedule the AHJ approves, so it stays in proper operating condition.
• (C) Battery systems: where battery systems or unit equipment are involved, periodic maintenance is required.
• (D) Written record: a written record of the tests and maintenance has to be kept.
• (E) Testing under load: means has to be provided to test the system under its maximum anticipated load.
The manufacturer instructions and industry standards fill in the details of how the equipment is maintained, but the NEC rule the inspector enforces is simple: test it, maintain it, and prove it on paper.
sections.on_the_job: At turnover on a Lake Nona outpatient clinic, Sharma left the owner a test binder, not just keys: the results of the AHJ-witnessed acceptance test, the periodic test schedule the AHJ approved, and the battery maintenance log with the first entries filled in. When the inspector asked how the system would be proven a year later, the answer was the binder — dates, loads, and signatures — not a promise that somebody would get around to it.

nec2023_change.change: Commissioning of the emergency system now has to be done or witnessed by the AHJ, and the hookup point for a temporary generator must be outdoors and fully labeled. The AHJ (authority having jurisdiction) has to commission the whole emergency system, or witness it, at startup and periodically after that (700.3(A)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 700.3 Emergency system commissioning

sections.why_it_exists: Emergency gear sits idle for months and is expected to work perfectly in the first seconds of the worst day. Batteries sulfate, fuel goes stale, transfer switches stick, and a system that is never tested under load fails silently: nobody finds out until the lights are already out and people are on the stairs. Scheduled testing with a written record is what turns a dormant installation into a proven system.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that testing is a one-time event the contractor performs alone at startup and reports afterward. 700.3(A) puts the AHJ in the acceptance test, conducting it or witnessing it, and (B) keeps the testing going on a schedule the AHJ approves. A system with no periodic testing and no written record is not a finished emergency system, however neatly it was wired.

sections.title: Capacity and rating — emergency systems
sections.plain_explanation:
Emergency equipment has to be suitable for the fault current available where it connects — gear that cannot safely carry or interrupt the fault it may see does not belong on a life-safety system. The system also has to have enough capacity for its emergency load, figured under Article 220 or by another method the AHJ approves.
• Capacity means every emergency load that operates at the same time, carried together.
• There is no user-selects-the-load shortcut here, the way there is for a manual optional standby system. On an emergency system the loads are fixed by the life-safety design, not picked at the switch.
• Selective coordination of the emergency overcurrent devices is a separate requirement, covered at 700.32.
sections.on_the_job: Take a two-story professional building in Winter Garden where the AHJ classes the egress system as emergency. The emergency loads are egress lighting at 6.4 kVA, exit signs at 0.5 kVA and the fire alarm system at 0.9 kVA — 7.8 kVA that all runs together, with nothing the user can shed. Run the Article 220 calculation before anyone promises a generator size, and check the fault-current rating on the transfer gear against the service: the marked rating has to cover the fault current available where the gear connects. If the quoted generator cannot carry the 7.8 kVA, that conversation happens at the quote, not at the first outage.

nec2023_change.change: Emergency capacity now has to cover transients and rapid load swings, and new rules spell out when an emergency source can run in parallel with the normal source or other emergency sources. Size the emergency system for all loads that run together, including rapid load swings and transients like motor starting (700.4(A)).

sections.why_it_exists: When the normal source fails, the emergency system is the only thing between the occupants and a dark stairwell. Gear that fails under fault current, or a source that sags because the load outgrew the calculation, turns a power outage into an evacuation problem. The capacity and rating rules make the system prove on paper, before the emergency, that it can carry every life-safety load at once and survive the worst fault at its terminals.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is sizing the emergency source the way a manual optional standby system is sized — letting the user pick which loads run and adding up only those. The second trap is checking only capacity and forgetting the rating half of the section; the equipment also has to be suitable for the available fault current.

sections.title: Transfer equipment — emergency systems
sections.plain_explanation:
700.5 sets the bar for transfer equipment on an emergency system — the gear that moves life-safety loads from the normal source to the emergency source.
• It must be automatic, listed and marked for emergency use, and approved by the AHJ.
• It must be built and installed so the emergency source and the other sources cannot be connected together by accident.
• An automatic transfer switch must be electrically operated and mechanically held — it stays on the source it is on; it does not drift or drop out.
• Reconditioned transfer switches are not allowed on an emergency system.
• The gear may feed only emergency loads. Standby and optional loads ride on their own equipment.
• Meter-mounted transfer switches are not permitted for emergency use — a device that is fine on a 702 dwelling job does not cross over to a 700 job.
• Documentation, 700.5(E): the transfer equipment short-circuit rating is field marked on the outside of the gear. The documentation rule of 700.5(E) carries no dwelling exception — unlike 702.5(C) — so the rating is marked in dwellings too.
sections.on_the_job: Small medical office in Kissimmee, 200 A service: the supplier quotes a meter-mounted transfer device because it is fast to install. It is rejected before rough-in — meter-mounted transfer switches are not permitted for emergency use, full stop. The job gets a Siemens 200 A automatic transfer switch listed and marked for emergency use (S-02), and before the inspector arrives the crew confirms the short-circuit rating is field marked on the outside of the enclosure, where 700.5(E) wants it — the plans show 22 kA of available fault current, and the marked rating has to cover it.
sections.sharma_note: S-02 applies to gear Sharma furnishes: new transfer equipment is Siemens. Listing and emergency marking still govern — brand never replaces either one.

sections.title: Signs — emergency sources
sections.plain_explanation:
A sign at the service equipment tells responders and electricians what kind of on-site emergency source the building has and where it is. Nobody should have to hunt through a building during an outage to learn that a second source exists.

The sign sits at the service equipment and states two things: the type of on-site emergency source and where that source is located. It has to be permanent and legible, and it is a different sign from the panel directory — the directory says which loads are emergency; this sign says a second source exists and where to find it. Where the source has its own disconnecting means away from the service, the sign at the service is what lets a responder find and kill both sources.
sections.on_the_job:
Put the source type and location on the sign and check it against the actual disconnect location before you call the job done.

Worked habit: letter the sign before final inspection, then stand at the service and check that a stranger could walk straight to the source from the words on it. A sign that says 'generator' but not where the generator is has not finished this section's job.

sections.title: Surge protection — emergency systems
sections.plain_explanation:
Every emergency system switchboard and panelboard has to have a listed surge protective device. This is a flat requirement of the article, not an upsell and not something to value-engineer out.
The device has to be listed, and it is installed in or on the switchboard or panelboard it protects, connected the way its listing and the manufacturer's instructions direct.
• Short, straight leads matter: a surge device works through its connection, and a long coiled lead-in adds impedance exactly where the surge arrives.
• A failed or end-of-life SPD that nobody notices leaves the panel unprotected while looking complete — which is why the device's status indication belongs on the 700.3 test-and-maintenance rounds.
sections.on_the_job: Small medical office in Lakeland: the emergency switchboard and one downstream emergency panelboard each get a listed SPD on the material list — two boards, two devices, no exception for the smaller panel. Each SPD mounts on the board it protects, with its leads kept as short and straight as the enclosure allows, and its status indicator goes on the 700.3 test log. The normal-power panels on the same job are a different conversation — 700.8 speaks only to the emergency system.
sections.why_it_exists: Florida lightning and utility switching throw surges onto service conductors every storm season. The emergency panel feeds the loads that protect life — egress lighting, exit signs, fire alarm — and those loads are electronic. One surge through an unprotected emergency board can kill the system on the day it is needed, and a silently dead SPD gives the same result behind a normal-looking panel. The rule puts a listed clamp on every board and a status check on the maintenance rounds.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is protecting the emergency switchboard and calling it done, because the surge 'hits the first board anyway.' Section 700.8 names switchboards and panelboards — every downstream emergency panelboard needs its own listed SPD. The other wrong answer is the unlisted device off the truck: the section's word is listed, and an unlisted SPD is a write-up, not protection.

sections.title: Wiring — emergency systems stay identified and apart
sections.plain_explanation: Emergency wiring is identified as emergency all the way through: boxes, enclosures, transfer switches, generators and panels are permanently marked, and emergency raceways and cables are marked as emergency at short, regular intervals. Emergency conductors also stay out of enclosures, raceways and cables that carry nonemergency wiring, with only narrow exceptions such as inside transfer equipment. Emergency receptacles are identified by a distinctive color or marking. The identification interval is concrete, not a judgment call: 700.10(A)(2) requires emergency wiring to be marked as emergency at intervals not exceeding 25 ft. And 700.10(D) adds fire protection for emergency feeders in the larger installations it covers — the feeder is protected by a listed electrical circuit protective system, mineral-insulated cable, concrete encasement, or an approved sprinkler-protected space, as the subsection conditions state.
sections.on_the_job: Mark it as you install it, not at trim-out from memory. If a normal circuit and an emergency circuit want the same raceway, stop — that is the exact mix this section exists to prevent.

sections.title: Sources of power — available in 10 seconds
sections.plain_explanation:
When the normal supply fails, emergency power has to be available within 10 seconds. The article lists the permitted kinds of sources, from storage batteries and generator sets to a separate service and unit equipment, and it sets conditions for each one. Engine-driven sources carry on-site fuel rules, battery sources carry a minimum run-time duty at close to full voltage, and the equipment has to be located and designed so one fire, flood or act of vandalism is less likely to kill both supplies at once.

Two numbers carry most of the field weight. A storage battery used as the emergency source has to carry the emergency load for at least 1-1/2 hours without its voltage dropping below 87-1/2 percent of nominal — a battery that fades at 40 minutes is not a 700 source, whatever its amp-hour label says. And the on-site fuel rule for engine-driven sets is part of the source itself: the fuel plan has to be there when the generator is, sized for the run the design requires, not improvised after the outage starts. an internal-combustion prime mover requires an on-premises fuel supply sufficient for not less than 2 hours of full-demand operation.

sections.on_the_job:
The 10-second clock is the design test. Ask how the source starts, how fast load lands on it, and where its fuel or charge comes from before you argue about brands.

Worked check on the battery duty: a battery string nameplated at 24 V nominal must still be holding at least 21 V (87.5 percent of 24) at the end of a 90-minute full-load run. If the acceptance test did not run the clock and read the voltage, the duty is unproven.

sections.title: Loads on emergency branch circuits
sections.plain_explanation:
Emergency branch circuits feed emergency loads only. A circuit that exists to keep egress lighting and exit signs alive does not pick up convenience loads because there was spare capacity on paper.
• Emergency loads are the life-safety loads classed as emergency by the governmental agency having jurisdiction: egress lighting, exit signs, fire alarm and similar loads.
• General receptacles, office and task lighting, comfort equipment and break-room appliances are not emergency loads, even when the generator is big enough to carry them.
• The limit is about what the load is, not about how much room is left on the circuit or in the panel.
Emergency wiring is identified as emergency as it runs through the building (700.10(A)), so a load that does not belong shows up on the panel schedule before it shows up in the field.
sections.on_the_job: Small medical office in Ocala: a Siemens emergency panel beside the normal panel, with six 20 A branch circuits carrying exit signs, egress lighting over the corridor and stairs, and the fire alarm. During the fit-out, a receptacle for the break-room coffee maker got landed on a spare emergency breaker because it was close. Walk the emergency panel schedule load by load. Anything that is not an emergency load comes off, even if the generator is big enough. The coffee-maker circuit moved to the normal panel before final.

sections.why_it_exists: The emergency source is sized, fueled and tested for one known list of life-safety loads. Every convenience load added to an emergency circuit steals capacity and run time from that list. The theft shows up at the worst moment: during a real outage, with the building occupied, the source overloads or runs short while people are still on the stairs.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is: the generator has capacity to spare, so one more receptacle circuit on the emergency panel is fine. 700.15 does not ration emergency circuits by capacity. It rations them by load type. If the load is not an emergency load, it does not go on an emergency branch circuit, however big the source is.

sections.title: Emergency illumination — no single failure leaves a space dark
sections.plain_explanation: Emergency illumination covers the means of egress lighting, the illuminated exit signs and every other luminaire specified as necessary to get people out. The system has to be designed and installed so that the failure of any single illumination source cannot leave a space that requires emergency illumination in total darkness — one dead lamp, ballast or driver never blacks out an exit path. Control devices on the system have to be listed for use in emergency systems. Where discharge lighting such as HID is the sole source of normal illumination, the emergency system has to operate until normal illumination is restored, because those lamps are slow to restrike. The section also requires emergency illumination in the area of an indoor service or feeder disconnecting means.
sections.on_the_job: Count sources, not fixtures on a schedule. Stand in each egress space and ask what goes dark if one source dies; if the answer is everything, the layout fails this section even though every fixture sits on an emergency circuit.

sections.title: Branch-circuit emergency lighting transfer switch (700.25)
sections.plain_explanation:
700.25 covers one device: the branch-circuit emergency lighting transfer switch. Where emergency lighting is served from a branch circuit, a listed transfer switch at the branch-circuit level is the device that moves that lighting load from the normal branch circuit to an emergency branch circuit when normal power fails, so the egress lighting does not depend on an upstream decision.
• The transfer happens out on the lighting circuit, not back at the service or at the main transfer switch.
• The loads it may transfer are emergency lighting loads on branch circuits rated not more than 20 A.
• The device is listed as transfer equipment. An automatic load control relay (700.26) is a different device: it can force emergency lights on, but it is not permitted to transfer a load between two sources.
It is a narrow, listed-device rule — the switch, its listing and its wiring follow the printed section and the design documents.
sections.on_the_job: Emergency-system design is engineered work. If a plan shows branch-circuit transfer switches for the egress lighting in a small Orlando office corridor, land them exactly as the drawings and the device listing say: normal feed in, emergency feed in, load out to the corridor lights. Flag any field change to the designer — do not re-feed egress lighting on your own call, and do not substitute a load control relay for a transfer switch. They are different devices with different listings, and only one of them may move a load between sources.

sections.title: Selective coordination — emergency systems
sections.plain_explanation:
Every overcurrent device in an emergency system has to selectively coordinate with all supply-side overcurrent protective devices. Selective coordination means that for any fault the system can deliver, only the device closest to the fault opens: the branch device clears a branch fault while the feeder and service devices stay closed.
• The coordination has to hold across the full range of overcurrents available at each point, not just at one fault level.
• A licensed professional engineer or another qualified person selects the devices and performs the coordination design.
• The coordination documentation has to be available to the people who design, install, inspect, maintain, and operate the system.
That is why a breaker swap or a settings change on an emergency system is an engineering event, not a parts swap.
sections.on_the_job: On a small medical office in Winter Park with a generator feeding a Siemens emergency distribution panel, the coordination study called out specific breaker frames and trip settings at the main, the feeder, and each branch. When the specified branch breaker was back-ordered, the crew did not substitute a same-ampere breaker from stock: a different trip curve can erase the coordination the study proved. The substitute waited for the engineer's written approval, and the study, device list, and settings went into the job record, where the owner and the AHJ can ask for them.

nec2023_change.change: Selective coordination on emergency systems now has to be rechecked after any overcurrent device replacement and after any change to the system. New 700.32(B): replace an emergency overcurrent device and coordination has to be reevaluated.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 700.32 Emergency selective coordination

sections.why_it_exists: An emergency system exists for the worst ten minutes of a building's life: a fire, a blackout, people feeling their way down the stairs. If a fault on one egress-lighting branch trips the emergency main instead of its own branch device, the whole building goes dark at the exact moment the system was installed to prevent. Selective coordination keeps a local fault local, so exit signs, fire alarm, and the rest of the egress lighting stay alive while the faulted branch is isolated.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that devices coordinate because their ampere ratings step down in size — a big main feeding a smaller feeder feeding a small branch breaker. Rating steps alone prove nothing. 700.32 requires the devices to be selected so that only the device protecting the faulted circuit opens, across the full range of overcurrents, and a qualified person has to design it and document it.

sections.title: Legally required standby systems — the middle tier
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 701 covers standby power that a law, code or AHJ requires, but that is not classed as emergency. These systems back up loads that aid firefighting and rescue, control health hazards, or keep ventilation, smoke removal, sewage, communications and similar loads running so an emergency does not get worse. They sit below Article 700 in priority: a 700 load always outranks a 701 load on a shared source. If nobody with authority required the system, it is not 701 — it is optional standby under 702.
• Speed: the power has to be available within 60 seconds of losing normal power — slower than 700's 10 seconds, but automatic, not “someone will start it eventually” (701.12).
• Capacity: the system carries its legally required loads; it may also carry 700 or 702 loads only with the capacity for them, or with automatic selective load pickup and shedding doing the sorting (701.4).
• Transfer equipment follows the 700 discipline: automatic, listed, approved, and marked for its short-circuit duty; reconditioned and meter-mounted transfer gear stay out (701.5).
• Wiring is the relaxed part: 701 wiring may share raceways and boxes with general wiring — the strict separation rule belongs to 700 (701.10).
sections.on_the_job: Picture a Marion County clubhouse where the county requires the sewage lift station and the smoke-control fans to stay up on an outage. That paperwork makes it 701, not 702: the generator and automatic transfer gear get sized for those loads, the power has to be on within 60 seconds, and — unlike a 700 job — the 701 feeders may share raceways with the general wiring on the way to the pumps. The egress lighting in the same building stays Article 700 and keeps its own separated wiring; one building can hold both tiers, and mixing their rules is the classic fail.

sections.why_it_exists: The middle tier exists because some loads are too important to leave to chance but are not egress life-safety loads: a sewage lift station that overflows into a Florida waterway, smoke-removal fans, a health-hazard process. If those loads wait for a portable generator and a long cord, the emergency they were meant to contain gets worse while everyone watches. The law required the backup, so the code makes it automatic, sized and tested — not a promise in a drawer.

sections.title: Transfer equipment — legally required standby
sections.plain_explanation:
Transfer equipment for a legally required standby system is held to a tighter standard than the same hardware on an optional standby job:
• It has to be automatic, listed and marked for legally required standby use, and approved by the AHJ.
• It has to keep the standby source from ever being interconnected with the normal source by accident — in any operation of the equipment, not just the normal switching sequence.
• Automatic transfer switches are electrically operated and mechanically held, so the contacts stay put if control power drops.
• Reconditioned transfer switches are not permitted.
• Meter-mounted transfer switches are not permitted on a 701 system either — that device belongs to 702 only.
• The transfer equipment short-circuit rating is field marked on the outside of the gear, where it can be read without opening the enclosure.
sections.on_the_job: Same discipline as Article 700: check the marking before the gear is ordered, not after it is hung. A charter school in Kissimmee adds a 60 kW standby generator for its legally required loads — egress lighting, fire alarm and the lift station. The switch is a new Siemens automatic transfer switch (S-02), ordered listed and marked for legally required standby use, with its short-circuit rating field marked on the enclosure. A cheaper reconditioned switch, and a meter-mounted switch quoted from a 702 house job, are both rejected at the desk. The 701 system also works to a 60-second availability clock (701.12), so the transfer has to be automatic — nobody is walking to the gear room to throw a handle.

If the transfer switch can parallel the generator with the utility, or a worn reconditioned switch fails halfway through a transfer, the protected load is the one that dies. Listing, marking and AHJ approval make the switch prove, before the outage, that it was built for this duty.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating 701 like 702: reaching for a meter-mounted transfer switch, or a reconditioned automatic switch at a better price. Both are permitted thinking on an optional standby job and both are prohibited here. The second trap is the holding method — the switch must be electrically operated and mechanically held, not electrically held, so a loss of control power cannot drop the contacts mid-event.

sections.title: Wiring — legally required standby may share raceways
sections.plain_explanation:
Unlike emergency wiring, legally required standby wiring is allowed to run in the same raceways, boxes and cabinets as general wiring. The strict separation duty belongs to Article 700: emergency conductors stay out of raceways, boxes and cables that carry nonemergency wiring, with only narrow exceptions, such as inside transfer equipment (700.10). Article 701 carries no such rule.
• Importing the 700 separation duty into a 701 job wastes raceways, boxes and labor the Code never asked for.
• Forgetting the separation on a 700 job is a violation.
• The wiring method follows the classification, so settle which article the system is under before the first raceway goes in.
sections.on_the_job: Community clubhouse in Marion County, with a sewage lift station and smoke-control fans on a legally required standby system. The standby feeder and the general feeders share the same raceway run out to the pump house. That is legal under 701.10, and it saved a second run. The same building's emergency lighting is Article 700 work, and those conductors stayed in their own raceway, start to finish. Know which article the job is under before you decide how to run the raceways. The wiring method follows the classification, not habit.

sections.title: Sources of power — available in 60 seconds
sections.plain_explanation:
Legally required standby power has to be available within 60 seconds of the normal supply failing — slower than the 10 seconds of Article 700, far faster than a portable generator someone drags out of a garage. The article lists the permitted source types and their conditions, including on-site fuel for engine-driven sources and battery duty where batteries are the source. One source may also carry optional loads only where capacity is truly there, or where automatic pickup and shedding protect the legally required loads first.

The battery duty mirrors the emergency tier: a storage battery source has to supply and maintain the legally required load for at least 1-1/2 hours without the voltage falling below 87-1/2 percent of nominal. Note that this chapter asks two different questions of a battery system — the 60-second availability clock above, and the 90-minute endurance duty here — and a system can pass one and fail the other.

sections.title: Selective coordination — legally required standby
sections.plain_explanation: Legally required standby overcurrent devices have to selectively coordinate with all supply-side overcurrent protective devices, so a fault on one standby branch opens the device at the fault instead of tripping devices upstream and darkening healthy standby loads with it. The coordination is selected by a licensed professional engineer or another qualified person engaged primarily in the design, installation or maintenance of electrical systems, and the selection has to be documented and made available to the people authorized to design, install, inspect, maintain and operate the system. It is the Article 700 duty at 700.32 carried one tier down. Coordination is not required between two devices in series where no loads are connected in parallel with the downstream device.
sections.on_the_job: Same discipline as the emergency tier: this is a study, not a field adjustment. Get the documented coordination selection into the job record before the gear is released, and leave it where the inspector and the owner's maintenance people can reach it.

sections.title: Optional standby systems — home and business generators
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 702 covers standby systems nobody required: the homeowner who wants the fridge, the well pump and a few lights through a Florida outage, or the business protecting product and comfort. Life safety does not depend on these systems, and that single fact is what keeps them out of Articles 700 and 701. The article still regulates them hard where it counts:
• Capacity: the system has to carry the loads connected to it, with load management where the design uses it (702.4)
• Transfer equipment: listed equipment that can never tie the generator to the utility by accident (702.5)
• Signs: a sign at the service equipment says a standby source is on the premises (702.7)
• Wiring, and the outdoor generator set rules, fill out the article
Portable generators that are never connected to the premises wiring are outside this article. The moment one is connected through an inlet and transfer equipment, 702 is in play.
sections.on_the_job: Most Sharma generator work lives here. Start every quote by sorting the loads into what runs automatically, what the owner will switch by hand, and what never runs on the generator. On a Marion Oaks house with a well, the must-run list reads: fridge 200 VA, well pump 1,800 VA, lights 900 VA, microwave 1,500 VA, TV and network gear 300 VA — 4,700 VA in all. A 6,500 W portable set on an inlet, through Siemens transfer equipment (S-02), carries that list with headroom. The range at 12,000 VA and the dryer at 5,600 VA stay off the generator list entirely.

sections.why_it_exists: Optional does not mean casual. A standby system connects a second source to a building that utility crews and firefighters expect to go dead when the service opens. A backfeed through a bad transfer setup can put full voltage on a line a crew believes is dead. The capacity, transfer and sign rules are what keep a comfort system from becoming the most dangerous wiring on the property.

If a governmental agency requires the system, or life safety depends on it, it is not optional: it lands in Article 700 or 701, with their separation, testing and 10-second rules. sections.title: Available fault current — optional standby equipment
sections.plain_explanation:
Optional standby equipment has to be suitable for the maximum available short-circuit current at its terminals. That is a different rating from the amp rating. A transfer switch can match the load exactly — 200 A switch on a 200 A service — and still be the wrong switch, because its short-circuit current rating sits below what the service can deliver into a fault.
• Get the available fault current before ordering: from the utility, or from the field marking on the service equipment. Other than in dwelling units, service equipment is marked with the maximum available fault current and the date it was figured (110.24).
• Compare that number with the short-circuit current rating marked on the transfer equipment, not with its amp rating.
• The same duty runs through the rest of the circuit: interrupting ratings (110.9) and the short-circuit current ratings of the components (110.10) must suit the fault current at their terminals.
sections.on_the_job: Strip-center tenant in Marion County: 200 A service, standby generator for the coolers and lights. The marking on the service gear read 22,000 A available fault current. The first transfer switch in the quote was a 200 A switch with a 10,000 A short-circuit rating: right amps, wrong fault duty, and it went back. The switch that stayed is rated 22,000 A. Pull the available fault current from the service gear or the utility information and match the transfer equipment rating to it before ordering, not at rough-in.

It draws everything the utility transformer can push until an overcurrent device clears, and the switch has to survive those cycles without welding its contacts shut or coming apart. sections.title: System capacity — the sizing fork in Article 702
sections.plain_explanation:
702.4(B) is the fork that decides how big an optional standby source has to be, and the fork is the transfer equipment.
• Manual transfer, 702.4(B)(1): the user stands at the switch and chooses the load. The source only has to supply the loads intended to be operated at one time — the user is the load management.
• Automatic transfer, 702.4(B)(2): nobody is standing there choosing, so the source is sized to the calculated load, figured under Article 220 or by another approved method. It must then either carry the full load the transfer equipment connects, or be paired with automatic load management that limits what gets connected.
There is no third branch. "Automatic transfer, partial load, no load management" is the combination this section exists to forbid. Which side of the fork a job is on gets decided on paper, before anything is sized or quoted.
sections.on_the_job: Two Marion County houses, same week. The first takes a portable 9 kW generator on a manual interlock: the owner's intended loads — refrigerator, well pump, a few lights and the TV — total about 7.5 kW at one time, so the source fits 702.4(B)(1). The second house wants a whole-home automatic switch: the Article 220 calculation comes to 24 kW, so the standby source is a 24 kW unit — or a smaller unit only if listed automatic load management is part of the design. Same street, two different sizes, and the transfer equipment is the whole reason.

sections.why_it_exists: A generator sized by optimism fails at the worst moment: the automatic switch transfers the whole house at 2 a.m. in a storm, the air conditioner and the well pump start together, and the undersized source stalls or trips — leaving the house dark and the food warm. The fork forces the sizing question to be answered by who chooses the load, not by what source happens to be on the truck.
sections.exam_trap: Exam writers love the middle answer: an automatic transfer switch with a generator sized to "the essential loads only" and no load management. That is not a legal configuration under 702.4(B)(2). With automatic transfer, the exits are the full calculated load or automatic load management — the homeowner's promise to behave is neither.

sections.title: Manual transfer — the user selects the load
sections.plain_explanation:
Where manual transfer equipment is used, the optional standby system has to be able to supply all the equipment intended to be operated at one time, and the user is permitted to select which loads are connected. That selection is what sets the practical size of the source: a homeowner who will run the fridge, a few lights and the well pump — and leave the range and dryer off — does not need a generator sized for the whole house.
• This is the manual-transfer fork of 702.4(B). Its twin, 702.4(B)(2), covers automatic transfer, where nobody stands there choosing: the source either carries the full calculated load or a load-management system does the choosing.
sections.on_the_job: Lake County house, manual transfer switch, owner's list agreed at the kitchen table: refrigerator 200 VA, well pump 1,800 VA, lights 900 VA, microwave 1,500 VA, TV and network gear 300 VA — 4,700 VA of intended load, all of it allowed to run at once. A 6,500 W portable covers the list with room to spare. The range at 12,000 VA and the dryer at 5,600 VA are not on the list, so they are not counted and not promised. The list goes in the job record, where the owner and the next tech both read the same deal.

sections.why_it_exists: A portable source is small, and a house is big. Without a written selection, every outage becomes an argument at the panel — someone adds the range, then the dryer, and the little unit drowns or the breaker does. The intended-load list turns the owner's choice into the design: the source is sized to a promise, and the promise is written down before the storm, not negotiated during it.

sections.title: Automatic transfer — full load, or load management
sections.plain_explanation:
Where automatic transfer equipment is used, 702.4(B)(2) sizes the standby source to the calculated load — figured under Article 220, or by another approved method. For an existing installation, recorded maximum demand is one of the approved routes the code recognizes through 220.87: real metered history instead of a fresh calculation.
The system then has to satisfy one of two duties:
• Full-load duty: the source carries the entire load the automatic equipment transfers. Nothing is shed and nothing is managed — the source is simply big enough.
• Load-management duty: an automatic system manages the connected load, and the source only has to carry the maximum load that management system will actually connect. Loads above that ceiling are shed or locked out by the equipment, not by the owner's good intentions.
Pick the duty on paper. The source size, the equipment list and the permit all have to tell the same story.
sections.on_the_job: Existing house in Ocala going whole-home automatic. The Article 220 calculation says 24 kW, and twelve months of utility demand history — the 220.87 route — backs up sizing from real use instead of the paper worst case. The design claims the load-management duty: a listed management system sheds the second air conditioner and the range, capping the connected load at 16 kW, and a 20 kW Siemens standby source carries it with margin. The management equipment is on the truck and on the permit — a load-management claim with no listed equipment on the job is just a smaller generator and a hope.
sections.why_it_exists: Automatic transfer happens with nobody home to make good choices — the switch moves the whole load the moment the utility drops. If the source cannot carry what the switch connects, the generator overloads and drops everything it was bought to save. Load management is the honest alternative: the equipment, not optimism, decides what runs.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is using the demand route or the management duty on the wrong job. Recorded maximum demand under 220.87 is a route for existing installations, not new work with no history. And the management duty is not the owner promising to turn things off — if the shedding is not automatic, the source must carry the full transferred load.

sections.title: Transfer equipment — required, listed, and built to keep sources apart
sections.plain_explanation:
Transfer equipment is required to connect an optional standby source to the premises wiring, and in the 2020 code it has to be listed — a tightening over earlier editions that catches unlisted interlock hardware.
• What counts: a listed transfer switch, or a listed interlock arrangement that mechanically keeps the normal source and the standby source from ever being connected at the same time.
• One narrow exception: a temporary portable generator connection without transfer equipment, only where maintenance and supervision ensure qualified persons service it and the normal supply is physically isolated by a lockable disconnect or by disconnecting the normal conductors.
The four duties that follow it in the section — meter-mounted transfer switches, documentation, inadvertent interconnection, and parallel operation — get their own pages next, in the section's own order.
sections.on_the_job: Marion Oaks house, 200 A Siemens panel, homeowner wants storm backup from a 12 kW portable generator. Sharma's answer is a listed Siemens interlock kit made for that panel and a 50 A inlet: the sliding plate lets the main and the generator breaker be on one at a time, never both. The homeowner's online 'universal' kit, tested only on someone else's panel, stays in its box — no listing, no install.

sections.why_it_exists: The transfer point is where a generator can kill someone it never meets. If generator power reaches the utility lines, a line worker on a pole blocks away can touch a conductor the utility has grounded and declared dead. Listed transfer equipment is tested to make that connection impossible; an unlisted kit is a promise nobody verified.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that an interlock kit 'tested to fit' your panel is good enough. Tested is not listed. 702.5 requires transfer equipment to be listed in the 2020 code, and the narrow no-transfer-equipment exception is for temporary portable connections under qualified supervision — not a permanent house hookup.

sections.title: Meter-mounted transfer switches
sections.plain_explanation:
A transfer switch that mounts in the meter socket — between the utility meter and its enclosure — is allowed for optional standby systems, but only as a listed meter-mounted transfer switch.
• Manual operation is the default: a meter-mounted switch is manual unless it is rated in accordance with the automatic-transfer sizing duty of 702.4(B)(2).
• The meter socket is not a loophole around generator sizing: automatic transfer still has to meet the same capacity rules as any other automatic switch, sized to the calculated load or paired with automatic load management.
• The contrast to remember: Articles 700 and 701 do not permit meter-mounted transfer switches at all. This device exists only in the optional standby world of Article 702.
sections.on_the_job: For a standby generator at a single-family home in Oviedo, the listed meter-mounted transfer switch kept the job simple: no separate transfer switch on the wall, and manual transfer — the homeowner starts the generator and transfers by hand. Because the switch was manual, the automatic sizing duty of 702.4(B)(2) never came into play. The utility still had to approve the work in its meter socket before the seal was cut, and that approval was separate from the county electrical inspection.
sections.why_it_exists: The meter socket is the one point where utility equipment, the service, and the premises wiring all meet, and it was never designed as a switch enclosure. A listed meter-mounted transfer switch is built and tested for that spot: interrupting service current and keeping the generator from ever backfeeding the utility. An unlisted gadget in the socket risks the life of a lineman working a line he was told was dead.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is 'permitted anywhere a transfer switch is permitted.' Meter-mounted transfer switches are an Article 702-only device: Articles 700 and 701 forbid them outright. The second trap is calling every meter-mounted switch automatic. It is manual unless it carries the rating 702.4(B)(2) demands for automatic operation.

sections.title: Documentation — short-circuit rating marked on the gear
sections.plain_explanation:
On jobs other than dwelling units, the short-circuit current rating of the transfer equipment has to be field marked on the outside of the equipment. Not inside the door, and not left in the submittal package: on the outside, where the next person to work on the gear sees it.
• The marking states the rating the equipment was installed for, so it is read off the equipment data after the 702.4(A) fault-current match is made.
• The person maintaining or replacing that gear years later should not need the original submittal to learn what fault duty it was built for.
• Dwelling units are the exception in this paragraph. The marking duty here is for other-than-dwelling work.

Carry a marker and the rating from the equipment data to every non-dwelling transfer install, and photograph the finished marking for the job record.

It also settles the question at final inspection in seconds: the rating is on the gear, in the open, or the job is not finished.

sections.title: Inadvertent interconnection — the heart of 702.5
sections.plain_explanation:
702.5(D) is the paragraph the whole transfer-equipment section hangs on:
• Transfer equipment has to be suitable for the use, listed, and designed and installed so that all sources of supply can never be inadvertently interconnected — in any operation of the equipment.
• "Any operation" includes the sloppy one nobody planned: a switch left mid-travel, a homeowner flipping breakers in the dark, an interlock installed wrong.
• This is the rule that kills backfeeding: a generator pushing power out through the service can energize a utility line that a line crew believes is dead.
• The listing requirement in this paragraph is the 2020 change — the unlisted interlock hardware that got by under older editions runs into it now.
sections.on_the_job: A homeowner in Ocala wants a portable-generator inlet for hurricane season on a 200 A Siemens service. Sharma's answer is listed transfer equipment — a listed transfer switch, or listed interlock hardware made for that panel — never a double-ended cord, and never a breaker held off by a zip tie and a label. After the install, the crew tests the finished job through every switch position, not just the normal one: normal, generator, and everything in between, confirming the utility and generator breakers can never be closed together. If the panel cannot take listed hardware, it gets a transfer switch beside it; the inlet alone is not a system.

sections.why_it_exists: Backfeed kills line workers. When a generator feeds a house panel without real transfer equipment, its power runs backward through the service and the utility transformer and comes out on the primary side at thousands of volts — on a line the crew has opened and believes is dead. The listed-equipment and never-interconnect rules exist so that no switch position, mistake or half-finished install can ever put the two sources together.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is "the two breakers are never on together because we labeled them." Labels and instructions are not transfer equipment. 702.5(D) demands equipment designed and installed so interconnection cannot happen in any operation — a mechanical impossibility built into listed hardware, not a promise written on the panel directory. The second trap is reading the rule as covering only the normal switching sequence; it covers every operation, including the wrong one.

sections.title: Parallel installation — Article 705 takes over
sections.plain_explanation:
Transfer equipment and electric power production systems installed to operate in parallel with the normal source also have to comply with Article 705.
• A standby source that only ever replaces the utility is a 702 job: transfer equipment, and no interconnection.
• The moment a source is meant to operate alongside the utility, the interconnection rules of Article 705 join the transfer rules.
• On a parallel job the two articles are not either/or: 702 governs the transfer, 705 governs the handshake with the live source.
sections.on_the_job: Ask one question on every generator quote: will this source ever run in parallel with the utility? A homeowner in Lake Mary wants a standby set that only takes over in an outage — that is a 702 job, priced and wired as transfer equipment. A small commercial customer who wants the generator to parallel the utility for peak shaving gets a different answer: the same transfer gear, plus an Article 705 interconnection — connection point, busbar and conductor checks, and marking that tells the next electrician a second source exists. Price and wire it as both, or do not sell it as parallel.

sections.why_it_exists: A source connected to a live utility system can backfeed conductors, fight the utility's protection, and keep a 'dead' service energized. Article 705 exists for exactly that handshake — where the source may connect, how much current the connection and the busbar may carry, and how the equipment is marked so the next person knows a second source exists. A parallel source wired to transfer rules alone skips every one of those protections.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating 702 and 705 as alternatives and picking one. On a parallel installation both apply: 702.5(E) sends you to Article 705 on top of the transfer rules. The reverse trap also fails — a standby source that never operates in parallel does not pick up Article 705 just because a generator is present.

sections.title: Signs — standby sources, and the power inlet sign
sections.plain_explanation:
Signs close the loop that transfer equipment starts.
• At service equipment, a sign identifies the type and location of each on-site optional standby source.
• For a house, the sign sits at the 230.85 emergency disconnect and points to the permanently installed standby source disconnect, or to the means to shut down the prime mover.
• Where a power inlet is used for a portable generator, a sign at the inlet states which kind of generator system may be connected there: a separately derived (bonded neutral) system only, or a nonseparately derived (floating neutral) system only.
Two signs, two different jobs — and the inlet sign cannot be lettered until somebody has checked how the generator's neutral is actually bonded.
sections.on_the_job: Marion Oaks house with a portable-generator inlet box on the garage wall. The service sign goes at the outdoor 230.85 emergency disconnect and reads where the standby source disconnect is. Before the inlet sign is lettered, the generator on site is checked: its neutral is bonded at the frame, so the inlet is lettered for a separately derived system only. Had the generator been a floating-neutral model, the same inlet would carry the opposite sign — same box, different words, decided by the machine, not the wall.

sections.why_it_exists: Standby power makes a building dangerous to anyone who thinks it is dead. A firefighter or the next electrician kills the service and still has a generator holding the panel up. The service sign tells them a second source exists and where to kill it. The inlet sign prevents the quieter mistake: the wrong neutral arrangement at a portable connection, which puts neutral current on grounding paths and defeats ground-fault protection.
sections.exam_trap: The common wrong answer letters the inlet sign from the transfer equipment, or copies the sign from the last job. The inlet sign states a property of the generator system — separately derived only, or nonseparately derived only. Letter it for the wrong neutral and the sign itself becomes the hazard, because the next generator that plugs in gets trusted on the strength of it.

sections.title: Wiring — optional standby wiring may share raceways
sections.plain_explanation:
Optional standby wiring is allowed to occupy the same raceways, cables, boxes and cabinets as other wiring. That permission is the opposite of the Article 700 rule, where emergency conductors stay independent of nonemergency wiring.
• The permission covers the whole run: raceways, cables, boxes and cabinets.
• It is one more reason the classification question comes first: the same physical run can be legal under 702 and a violation under 700.
• The permission is not a shortcut around the identification, transfer equipment and sign rules elsewhere in this article. It answers only the raceway question.
• Sharing the raceway does not merge the systems. The standby circuits still have to be findable later, which is why they stay identified in the panel directory.
sections.on_the_job: New slab home in Ocala with a permanently installed standby generator on a 200 A Siemens service. The generator feeder shares the underground run and the panel gutter with the normal circuits. That is permitted under 702.10, and it kept the job to one trench. Use the permission, but keep the standby circuits identified in the panel directory so the next electrician knows what the generator feeds: refrigerator, well pump and kitchen lights, marked as standby circuits in the directory.

sections.why_it_exists: Optional standby protects property and comfort: the fridge, the well pump and a few lights through a Florida outage. Nobody's escape route depends on it, so the Code does not buy it the expensive protection of separate raceways. The danger Article 702 does police is different — a generator tied to the utility by accident — and that is handled by the transfer equipment rules, not by separation.

sections.title: Outdoor portable generators
sections.plain_explanation: 702.11 covers the portable generator that lives in the garage and rolls out to the driveway when the power fails. The disconnect relief is exact: under 702.11(B), a portable generator rated 15 kW or less, connected through a flanged inlet or other cord-and-plug connection, does not need an additional disconnecting means where its ungrounded conductors serve or pass through a building. Under 702.11(A), permanently installed generators and portable generators over 15 kW need a readily accessible disconnect per 445.18, within sight of the building, for that relief. The connection to the house is still through listed transfer equipment and a proper power inlet (702.12(C) covers inlets 100 A and up); a cord through a window to a dryer receptacle is backfeeding, not a connection method. The neutral question decides the transfer equipment: whether the portable set's neutral is bonded to its frame determines whether the transfer switch must switch the neutral, and the generator's documentation — not habit — answers it.
sections.on_the_job: Hurricane setup: inlet box on the outside wall, listed transfer equipment or an interlocked breaker inside, generator outdoors and clear of windows and doors while it runs. Check the set's neutral bonding before you choose the transfer switch, and label the inlet for the size of set it accepts.

sections.title: Outdoor generator sets — when a building disconnect is not required
sections.plain_explanation:
702.12 is about not duplicating a disconnect that already does the job.
• For permanently installed generators and portable generators over 15 kW used outdoors, if the generator has a readily accessible disconnect within sight of the building it supplies, no extra disconnect is required at the building — provided that generator disconnect is in accordance with 445.18, and where the generator supply conductors terminate at a disconnecting means in or on the building, that disconnect meets 225.36.
• For a portable generator of 15 kW or less connected through a flanged inlet or another cord-and-plug connection, no disconnecting means is required at the building for the ungrounded conductors serving or passing through it.
Within sight has a code meaning: visible and not more than 50 ft away. Neither rule removes the transfer-equipment duty in 702.5.
sections.on_the_job: Whole-house standby set on a pad outside a Marion Oaks home: the generator's own disconnect is readily accessible and 22 ft from the house, in plain view of it, so no second disconnect goes on the building. The crew still checks the two conditions before relying on that — disconnect per 445.18, and the building disconnect where the supply conductors land meets 225.36. On the next job, a 12 kW portable on a flanged inlet needs no building disconnect for its ungrounded conductors at all.
sections.why_it_exists: A second disconnect nobody needs adds cost and one more thing to maintain, but the relief only works if the generator's own disconnect is genuinely there — reachable in a hurry and close enough to see from the building. The conditions are the safety case: accessible, within sight, and built to the generator and outdoor-feeder rules.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is 'outdoor generators never need a building disconnect.' The relief is conditional: over 15 kW it needs the generator disconnect readily accessible and within sight — visible and not more than 50 ft — and per 445.18. The second trap is thinking 702.12 relief waives transfer equipment; 702.5 still applies in full.

sections.title: Power inlets 100 A and up — listed, with an interlocked disconnect
sections.plain_explanation:
Where a portable generator connects through an inlet rated 100 amps or more, the 2020 code adds two requirements on the inlet equipment.
• The equipment must be listed for the intended use.
• It must be provided with an interlocked disconnecting means, so the inlet arrangement cannot leave the building connected the wrong way.
Two exceptions soften it: the inlet device itself may serve as the disconnecting means where it is rated for that duty, and supervised industrial installations with a permanent generator space within line of sight follow their own conditions. Below 100 amps this paragraph does not apply — the 702.12(A) and (B) rules on the previous page govern instead.
sections.on_the_job: Small commercial dock in Leesburg takes storm power from a portable generator through a 100 A inlet. Before any conductor lands, the crew reads the inlet's listing and works the interlocked disconnect through its positions: inlet live only in the generator position, building isolated from the utility in that same move. If either the listing or the interlock is missing at 100 A, the job stops at the dock — it is a stop-and-call, not a field fix.

sections.why_it_exists: At 100 amps and up, a portable hookup moves serious energy through a connection someone makes by hand, often in the dark after a storm. The interlock makes the wrong connection physically impossible instead of merely against the rules, and the listing proves the inlet gear was tested for generator duty.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is applying this paragraph to every inlet. The listing-plus-interlock duty starts at 100 A; below that, 702.12(A) and (B) govern. The other trap runs the opposite way: calling any inlet a disconnect. The inlet device may serve as the disconnecting means only where it is rated for that duty.

sections.title: Interconnected electric power production sources
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 705 governs sources that operate in parallel with another source — most often a solar inverter, storage system or generator tied to a live utility service. It answers three practical questions: where may the source connect, how much current may the connection and the busbar carry, and how does everyone after you know the extra source exists.
• Connections land on the supply side under 705.11 or the load side under 705.12, and a power control system under 705.13 can change the math.
• On the load side, the busbar rules in 705.12(B)(3) cap the backfeed: with the sources at opposite ends of the bus, 125 percent of the source output plus the rating of the device protecting the busbar must not exceed 120 percent of the busbar rating.
Article 690 in Chapter 6 governs the solar array itself; this article governs its handshake with the premises wiring.
sections.on_the_job: An Orlando homeowner adds a 7.6 kW solar inverter to a 200 A Siemens panel with a 200 A main. The load-side math: 120 percent of the 200 A busbar is 240 A; minus the 200 A main leaves 40 A of room, and the inverter's 32 A output at 125 percent is exactly 40 A — it fits, with the backfed breaker at the opposite end of the bus and its do-not-relocate label. The same house with a 10 kW inverter needs 52.5 A of room at 125 percent (42 A output), which this panel does not have: the choice becomes a supply-side connection under 705.11 or a power control system under 705.13, decided on paper before anyone drills.

sections.why_it_exists: A panel busbar was built and tested for current entering at one point. A second source feeding the same bus can push a section of that bus past its rating without any single breaker seeing an overload — the bar overheats quietly inside a closed panel. Article 705 exists to keep the combined math honest, and to make sure the next person who opens the panel knows a second source is there.

Put the backfed breaker next to the main and the plain 100 percent method in 705.12(B)(3)(1) governs instead.

sections.title: Identification of power sources — the directory
sections.plain_explanation:
Where sources are interconnected, 705.10 makes somebody write down where the power can come from:
• A permanent plaque or directory is installed at the service equipment, or at another approved, readily visible location.
• It shows the location of the disconnect for every parallel power source — every source that can feed the building alongside the service.
• It carries the caution that multiple sources of power are present.
• Any diagram on the plaque has to be oriented the way the building actually sits — the garage on the plaque is the garage on the ground.
This is the page a firefighter or a utility worker reads at 2 a.m. It has to be right, not approximate.
sections.on_the_job: A Winter Park house gets a roof array and a battery in the garage on a 200 A Siemens service. Before the plaque is engraved, the Sharma lead walks the property with the plan in hand: service disconnect at the meter, PV disconnect beside the inverter in the garage, battery disconnect on the garage wall by the door. The plaque at the service lists all three, with a site diagram drawn the way the lot actually sits — house front to the street, garage on the left. The inverter moved two studs during the install, so the plaque shows where it is, not where the plan put it.

sections.title: Supply-side source connections
sections.plain_explanation:
A source may connect on the supply side of the service disconnect, at the points the service rules allow, under its own set of conditions for conductor sizing, overcurrent protection and grounding. A supply-side connection steps around the panelboard busbar limits entirely, which is why it is the escape route when the 120 percent math in 705.12 will not close. It trades that freedom for service-level work: the connection is ahead of the main, so its protection and its disconnecting means have to be planned like service equipment. Two consequences follow in the field:
• There is no busbar sum to pass — but the conductors from the tap to the source disconnect are sized and protected as the section requires, and the disconnect is located, grouped and marked the way service disconnects are.
• The utility is part of the job: the tap is made on their side of the main, so coordination and a meter pull are scheduled, not improvised.
sections.on_the_job: An Ocala house with a 200 A panel gets a 9.6 kW PV array — 40 A of inverter output. The load-side math will not close: the panel is full, and there is no legal landing spot for the backfed breaker. Sharma prices the supply-side route instead: a tap between the meter and the main, a 50 A fused disconnect — 125 percent of the 40 A continuous output — mounted with the service equipment and marked as a PV service disconnect, conductors sized for the source, and a scheduled meter pull with the utility. Priced as service work with utility coordination, not as 'one more breaker.'

The 2020 inside-building length limits dropped out. Conductors from the tie-in to the power source's disconnect are service conductors now, and that disconnect is a service disconnect located like one (230.70(A)).

sections.title: Load-side source connections — the shape of the rule
sections.plain_explanation:
A source output may connect on the load side of the other source's service disconnect, at any distribution equipment on the premises. That freedom is what 705.12 spends its sub-rules controlling. Where the equipment is fed by two sources at once and feeds branch circuits or feeders, work the list in order:
• A dedicated breaker or fusible disconnect for each source, 705.12(A). Two inverters never share one device, and a source never lands on a breaker that also feeds a load.
• Conductor and busbar ampacity, 705.12(B). For a busbar, one of the (B)(3) methods must pass: the 100 percent method (125 percent of source output plus the rating of the device protecting the busbar must not exceed the busbar rating — the breaker may sit anywhere), the 120 percent rule (the same sum may reach 120 percent of the busbar, with the sources at opposite ends), the sum-of-breakers method, or the center-fed method.
• Marking of equipment that contains more than one source, so the next person knows it can be live from two directions.
• Breakers suitable for backfeed, and fastening where a backfed breaker could work loose — a plug-in breaker feeding the bus needs a hold-down.
Where a power control system is installed under 705.13, the controller setting stands in for the source output current in these calculations.
sections.on_the_job: Rooftop solar on a Marion Oaks house, 200 A Siemens panel with a 200 A main. The inverter's maximum continuous output is 32 A. Under the 120 percent rule the sum may reach 240 A — 120 percent of the 200 A bus — so 125 percent of the inverter output, 40 A, lands exactly at the cap: 200 + 40 = 240. The solar breaker goes at the opposite end of the bus from the main, gets its hold-down kit, and the panel gets its multi-source warning label. Under the 100 percent method this same inverter would not fit at all — position is what buys the room.

The 705.12 methods are thermal bookkeeping: they keep the bus from becoming the fuse. The marking and hold-down rules protect the next person — a backfed breaker that pops loose, or a panel nobody warned about, is how a "dead" bus stays live.
sections.exam_trap: The classic trap puts the solar breaker anywhere it fits and still claims the 120 percent rule. Position is part of the method: 120 percent buys its extra room only with the sources at opposite ends of the bus. A breaker that may sit anywhere means the 100 percent method — and there the sum may not exceed the busbar rating itself.

sections.title: Dedicated overcurrent and disconnect — each source gets its own
sections.plain_explanation:
Each source interconnection is made at its own dedicated circuit breaker or fusible disconnecting means. Two inverters do not share one breaker because the math happened to fit, and a source does not land on a breaker that also feeds a load.
• One source system, one dedicated device — every time.
• The dedicated device is both the overcurrent protection point for the interconnection and the place that source is disconnected.
• A breaker that feeds loads is never an interconnection point, and a source breaker never doubles as a load breaker.
sections.on_the_job: A small commercial rooftop in Clermont gets two string inverters: one with a 32 A maximum output current, one with 16 A. On the takeoff that is two dedicated breakers in the panel — a 40 A for the first inverter and a 20 A for the second, each sized from its own inverter's continuous output, and neither breaker feeds anything else. When a panel schedule shows one 60 A breaker with both inverters landed on it because the total 'fit,' send it back: 705.12(A) counts sources, not sums.

Open the wrong device and a source is still backfeeding the panel while someone works in it; trip one shared device and two sources drop together, or a source ends up protected at a rating that has nothing to do with its own output. A dedicated device per source makes each source visible, protected at its own rating, and disconnectable on its own.

The second trap lands a source on a breaker that also feeds a load; a dedicated device serves its source and nothing else.

sections.title: The 100 percent busbar method — breaker anywhere
sections.plain_explanation:
The plainest load-side method: 125 percent of the source output current, plus the rating of the overcurrent device protecting the busbar, must not exceed the busbar ampacity itself. Meet that sum and the source breaker may sit anywhere on the bus. Fail it and you do not argue with the arithmetic — you move to one of the other methods in 705.12(B)(3), derate something, or go to the supply side.
Worked on the example from the lookup entries: a 225 A bus protected by a 200 A main leaves 25 A of room in the sum. At 125 percent, that room is a 20 A source output. One amp more of output and this method is done, even though the panel still has empty spaces.
sections.on_the_job: Run this method first because it is the one with no position condition. On a Winter Garden house: 225 A bus, 200 A main. The sum leaves 225 − 200 = 25 A, so the largest source this method takes is a 20 A inverter output — 125 percent of 20 A is 25 A, and 200 + 25 = 225, exactly the bus. The customer wants a 32 A inverter instead: 125 percent is 40 A and the sum is 240 A, which fails here. That is not a dead end. The 120 percent method on the next page allows 120 percent of 225 A, or 270 A, so the same 240 A sum passes there — with the source breaker at the opposite end of the bus and its warning label in place.

sections.why_it_exists: A busbar fed by two sources can carry the utility current and the source current at the same time, and the bus sees the sum. Breakers trip on their own current, not on the total flowing through the bus under them, so an unchecked sum overheats the bus in silence. The 100 percent method is the conservative answer: if the worst-case sum can never beat the bus rating, breaker position stops mattering.

sections.exam_trap: The trap is feeding the sum the wrong current: candidates plug in the inverter's breaker size, or its nameplate output without the 125 percent. The method takes 125 percent of the source output current, every time. Second trap: comparing the sum to 120 percent of the bus on this method. The 100 percent method compares the sum to the busbar ampacity itself — 120 percent belongs to the methods that control breaker position.

sections.title: The 120 percent rule — sources at opposite ends
sections.plain_explanation: Where two sources sit at opposite ends of a busbar that carries loads, the same sum — 125 percent of the source output current plus the rating of the device protecting the busbar — may go up to 120 percent of the busbar ampacity. The busbar still has to be sized for the connected loads under Article 220. Because the allowance depends on position, a permanent warning label goes on the distribution equipment next to the backfed breaker, warning that it is a power source output connection and must not be relocated. On the common 200A bus with a 200A main, this method allows 40A of backfeed device capacity, which is a 32A inverter output — the worked example already in v1 as L-092 and Q-063.
sections.on_the_job: Three field checks, every time: sources truly at opposite ends, the math done with 125 percent of output (not the breaker size), and the do-not-relocate label on before inspection. Moving that breaker 'a couple of spaces' on a later service call quietly breaks the method.
sections.sharma_note: S-03 matters here on existing work: in an existing Square D panel, the backfed breaker is a Square D breaker listed for that panel — the 120 percent math never licenses a mixed-brand breaker.

sections.title: The sum-of-breakers method
sections.plain_explanation:
705.12(B)(3)(3) is a third load-side method for connecting a power source to a panelboard, and it works by counting breakers instead of trusting the main:
• Add up the ampere ratings of all the overcurrent devices on the panelboard — load devices and supply devices together.
• Leave out only the overcurrent device that protects the busbar itself.
• The total must not exceed the ampacity of the busbar.
• Equipment using this method carries permanent warning labels at the distribution equipment identifying that all sources are present.
It fits panels where the breaker population, not the main breaker rating, is the honest limit on the bus.
sections.on_the_job: A 200 A Siemens panel in a Clermont home gets a solar supply breaker, and the crew counts what is actually in the panel, including the source breaker: load breakers totaling 170 A plus the new 40 A supply breaker is 210 A — over the 200 A busbar, so this method fails as built. The honest fixes are removing breakers that are genuinely spare, downsizing the supply breaker, or using a different 705.12(B)(3) method — worked out before the inspection, with the sum written in the job record. A panel that passes today can fail this method after one added circuit, so the count gets done again at every addition.

sections.why_it_exists: A busbar does not care which breaker fed it — it carries the sum of everything connected to it. A panel can respect its main breaker rating and still be overfed once a supply breaker is added on top of a full row of load breakers. The sum-of-breakers method caps the total iron on the bus, and the warning labels tell the next electrician that more than one source can feed the panel.

The method excludes only the device protecting the busbar, and it counts every other overcurrent device, load and supply together, against the busbar ampacity. The second trap is treating the count as a one-time event: the method is re-tested every time a breaker is added to the panel.

sections.title: The center-fed busbar method — one end only
sections.plain_explanation: Some dwelling panelboards are center-fed: the main breaker or main lugs sit in the middle of the busbar instead of at one end, a construction common on combination meter-and-panel equipment in some regions. This method permits a source connection at either end of that busbar, but never at both ends. The math is the familiar 120 percent check applied to the connection: the sum of 125 percent of the power source output circuit current and the rating of the overcurrent device protecting the busbar must not exceed 120 percent of the busbar rating. Because a center-fed bus can concentrate load on one half of the busbar, the option is limited to dwellings.
sections.on_the_job: Identify the panel construction before reaching for the 120 percent rule: if the main sits in the middle, this paragraph is the method, not (3)(2). Land the source at one end only, run the math on that connection, and record which end was used in the job file.

sections.title: Power control systems — a listed controller can limit the current
sections.plain_explanation:
New in the 2020 code, this section recognizes a power control system: listed equipment that monitors and limits how much current a source puts onto conductors and busbars. Where one is installed, its controller setting is treated as the source output current for the 705.11 and 705.12 calculations, so a system set to a lower limit can fit a panel the raw inverter rating could not. The 2020 rules around the controller:
• Monitoring, 705.13(A): the controller must monitor all current within the system. A busbar or conductor it does not monitor is sized under 705.12 the ordinary way.
• Settings, 705.13(B): the PCS currents plus the other monitored source currents may not exceed the ampacity of any busbar or conductor they supply.
• Overcurrent protection, 705.13(C): the system must provide it, by devices or by its own listing.
• Access, 705.13(E): settings are restricted to qualified personnel — sealed covers, bolted or locked doors, or a password (240.6(C)).
sections.on_the_job: A Kissimmee house has a 200 A Siemens panel with a 200 A main and a 200 A bus. The PV inverter's nameplate output is 40 A, so the ordinary 705.12 sums fail: 125 percent of 40 A is 50 A, and 200 + 50 = 250 A beats even the 120 percent method's 240 A cap. The design instead uses a listed power control system set to 32 A. The setting stands in for the source output current: 125 percent of 32 A is 40 A, and 200 + 40 = 240 A — exactly the 120 percent cap, with the source breaker at the opposite end of the bus. The 32 A setting is recorded on the plans, marked at the panel, and locked behind the controller password.
