sections.title: Disconnecting means for sources
sections.plain_explanation:
Every interconnected power source — PV inverter, battery system, generator tying in under this article — needs its own disconnecting means that meets this section. In 2020 the source disconnect rules were gathered into this one place.
• The disconnect has to separate the source from the conductors of the other systems, opening all the ungrounded conductors at the same time.
• It has to be readily accessible and operable from outside without exposing the operator to live parts.
• It has to plainly show whether it is open or closed — no guessing from the handle position alone.
• Its ratings have to suit the load it carries and the fault current available where it lands.
• Where both sides of the disconnect can stay energized, the equipment carries a warning — a source can feed a panel from the far end.
• Under the 2020 rule, an enclosure cover on a disconnect that unqualified people can reach has to be locked or need a tool to open where opening it would expose live parts.
sections.on_the_job: On a Palm Coast house with rooftop PV and a battery inverter landing in the same Siemens panel, land each source on its own disconnect where the 705.10 directory at the service says it is, so the next person can find both without opening the house. Check the open-position condition before you call it done: open the disconnect and meter both sides. The line side from the panel can still be live, and the source side can wake up when the sun hits the array — terminals that stay live get the warning label the equipment rules call for.

sections.why_it_exists: A second source turns “I opened the breaker” into a lie. A panel fed by the utility and a battery or PV inverter can stay live from the far end after the normal disconnect is open, and the person who finds out is usually holding a meter lead or a pair of cutters. This section exists so every source has one known, visible, rated way to separate it — and so nobody has to trust that a silent panel is a dead panel.

sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: one main disconnect ahead of the panel separates everything, so the sources behind it need nothing of their own. Wrong — 705.20 wants a disconnecting means for the source itself, separating that source from the other systems' conductors. A shared switch that leaves the inverter tied to a live bus has not separated anything.

sections.title: Overcurrent protection — interconnected sources
sections.plain_explanation:
Conductors and equipment on an interconnected system get overcurrent protection under 705.30, working with the circuit-current sizing in 705.28 and with Article 240.
• Protection from all sources (705.30(A)). A conductor fed from both ends can be overcurrented from either direction, so protection is planned for the source output the same way it is planned for a utility feed.
• Device ratings follow the calculated source currents. The source output current is the nameplate current (705.28), and conductors and overcurrent devices are sized at not less than 125% of that maximum current — the continuous-output factor is built in.
• Equipment containing overcurrent devices supplied from more than one power source is marked to indicate that all sources are present (705.30(C)).
• A circuit breaker not marked line and load is suitable for backfeed; one marked line and load is not (705.30(D)).
sections.on_the_job: On a small commercial rooftop in Orlando, the interactive inverter's nameplate continuous output is 32 A. Sharma sizes the output conductors and the backfed breaker at 125% — 32 × 1.25 = 40 A — using a Siemens 40 A breaker that is not marked line and load. The panelboard is marked for multiple sources, because that panel is now fed from two directions and the next person who opens it needs to know.

Protection planned only around the utility feed leaves the conductor exposed to the inverter or generator feeding it backwards, and fault current does not care which end it came from. The marking and backfeed rules exist because the second source is invisible until somebody opens the wrong device.

Source output conductors protected at the utility end only, with nothing protecting them from the source end (705.30(A)).

The inverter does limit its current, but 705.28 still requires conductors and protection at not less than 125% of the maximum source current. Skipping the factor is the classic wrong answer — and so is landing a line/load-marked breaker where it will be backfed.

sections.title: Loss of primary source — the source must stop and stay off
sections.plain_explanation: When the primary source — normally the utility — is lost, an interconnected power production source has to be automatically disconnected from all ungrounded conductors of the primary source, and it must not reconnect until the primary source is restored. The duty bites even if only one line or phase of the utility supply opens. It exists so a solar array or cogeneration source can never backfeed lines that utility crews are treating as dead. The exception is the listed utility-interactive inverter: it may keep producing ac power for local loads as long as no power reaches the service conductors, which in effect turns the premises into their own island. A source serving an emergency or legally required standby system through transfer equipment is not shut down by this section — those systems are supposed to run during the outage.
sections.on_the_job: This is why a grid-tied inverter goes quiet in an outage even in full sun: it is not broken, it is obeying this section. If the owner wants power during outages, the answer is equipment designed to island legally, never a defeated anti-islanding control.

sections.title: Energy storage systems — batteries under the code
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 706 covers energy storage systems over 1 kWh that can feed a premises wiring system, on their own or alongside other sources.
• Only qualified persons install and maintain these systems.
• Each system is listed, and its nameplate carries the ratings the installer and the inspector both work from.
The two hazards that shape the article are stored energy that is still live when everything looks off, and fault current a battery bank can deliver without any utility behind it. Dwellings get extra attention: the disconnect a first responder can reach, and a dc voltage limit inside the home — 100 volts between conductors or to ground, with up to 600 volts allowed where live parts are not accessible during routine maintenance (706.20(B)).
sections.on_the_job: Garage wall of a Marion Oaks house: a listed ESS cabinet, nameplate rated over 1 kWh, goes in with its disconnect where a first responder walking up the driveway can reach it. Before landing a single conductor, the crew meters the battery terminals — the inverter display says off, and the meter is the only opinion that counts. The bank's dc voltage stays under the 100 V dwelling limit with its live parts as installed.
sections.figure_idea: Original diagram: a battery cabinet, an inverter and a panel, with a bold disconnect symbol between the batteries and everything else, and a 'stored energy stays live' callout on the battery side.
sections.florida_note: Florida note: hurricane-driven battery work is arriving in houses that were never designed for it. The ESS rules in this article, plus the fire-code siting the AHJ enforces, both apply — ask the AHJ about location limits before the batteries are set.
sections.why_it_exists: A battery does not go dead when you open a switch — the energy is still in the cabinet, and a shorted bank can deliver enormous fault current with no utility behind it. That is why the article insists on listed systems, qualified hands, a nameplate everyone works from, and a disconnect a firefighter can find in the dark.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is quoting 600 V as the dwelling limit. Inside a home the limit is 100 V dc between conductors or to ground; 600 V is allowed only where live parts are not accessible during routine maintenance. The second trap is trusting the inverter's 'off' state — stored energy is live until a meter proves otherwise.

sections.title: Commissioning and maintenance — energy storage
sections.plain_explanation:
Away from one- and two-family dwellings, an energy storage system is commissioned when it is installed. Every system — dwellings included — is kept maintained in proper and safe operating condition, following the manufacturer instructions and industry standards.
• Commissioning proves the installed system works as a system: connections, controls and protective functions checked and documented at installation.
• Maintenance is not optional, and it is not guesswork: the manufacturer's instructions set the tasks.
• Storage is not fit-and-forget equipment: connections, ventilation, controls and firmware all age.
sections.on_the_job: Sharma wires a listed battery system — over 1 kWh, so Article 706 applies — at a small warehouse in Orlando. Because it is not a one- or two-family dwelling, the system is commissioned at installation: operation verified, settings and protective functions checked, and the commissioning record written up. Hand over the commissioning record and the maintenance instructions with the job. If the owner cannot say who maintains the system, that conversation happens at sale, not at the first fault.

sections.why_it_exists: A battery system stores enough energy to hurt someone on a day when every switch looks off. Connections loosen and heat, ventilation gets blocked by stored material, firmware and protective settings drift — and none of it announces itself until the system is asked to perform, or fails hot. Commissioning catches the installation errors on day one; maintenance catches the aging before it becomes a fire or a dead system.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating commissioning as a rule for every installation. In the 2020 text the commissioning duty stops at one- and two-family dwellings — but the maintenance duty does not: a dwelling system still has to be maintained in proper and safe operating condition. The second trap: 'commissioned' does not mean 'turned on once.' It means tested, verified and documented.

sections.title: Disconnecting means — energy storage systems
sections.plain_explanation:
A disconnecting means has to separate the storage system from the other power sources, the utilization equipment and the premises wiring, and integral disconnects in listed equipment can do that job. The disconnect is readily accessible, at the system or within sight of it, it plainly shows whether it is open or closed, and it is permanently marked as the energy storage system disconnect, with the system's nominal ac voltage, maximum dc voltage and available fault current marked where the section requires them. For a house, the disconnect or its remote control sits at a readily accessible spot outside the building, where responders can reach it. The marking package in 706.15 also calls for an arc-flash warning label, and where the label is based on an arc-flash hazard analysis it carries the date that analysis was performed. Items (2), (3) and (4) of that marking list are waived for energy storage systems in one- and two-family dwellings.

sections.title: Circuit sizing and overcurrent protection — storage circuits
sections.plain_explanation:
Storage circuit currents come from the nameplate ratings (706.30(A)), and the rest of the sizing follows from them:
• For an ESS circuit, use the nameplate-rated current. For an inverter, use its continuous output current on the ac side, and its continuous input current at the lowest input voltage on the dc side.
• Conductors must have an ampacity at least the greater of the nameplate current or the rating of the overcurrent device protecting them (706.30(B)).
• The overcurrent protection that follows in 706.31 must be rated not less than 125% of the 706.30 current, unless the assembly, overcurrent devices included, is listed for operation at 100% of its rating (706.31(B)).
• On the dc side, devices must be listed for dc use, with the appropriate voltage, current and interrupting ratings (706.31(C)). Battery circuits punish borrowed ac-only habits: a device that cannot interrupt dc fault current is not protection, whatever its amp number says.
sections.on_the_job: On a solar-plus-storage house in Winter Garden, the ESS inverter's nameplate continuous output is 40 A, so the ac breaker is 50 A — 40 × 1.25 — and the conductors are sized to that breaker, not to the 40 A nameplate. On the dc side, read the dc rating on every fuse and breaker in the battery circuit out loud during the rough-in inspection of your own work. If it does not say dc, it comes out.

sections.why_it_exists: A battery bank is a fault-current machine sitting inside the building: very high available fault current at its terminals, and dc has no zero crossing to help a device put out an arc. A breaker chosen by amp number alone can weld shut on dc fault current, leaving the circuit defended on paper only — inches from the largest energy source on the job.
inspection_fails: AC-rated breaker installed on the battery dc circuit — not listed for dc use (706.31(C)).
Overcurrent device sized at nameplate current with no 125% factor, and the assembly is not listed for 100% operation (706.31(B)).
Conductors sized to the nameplate current but smaller than the rating of the overcurrent device protecting them (706.30(B)).
DC fuse with an interrupting rating below the battery bank's available fault current.
sections.exam_trap: Two wrong answers live here. First: the battery breaker at exactly the 40 A nameplate current, because the inverter limits its output — 706.31(B) wants not less than 125% unless the assembly is listed for 100% operation. Second: an ac-rated breaker on the dc side because the amp number matched. On a battery circuit, the amp number is the least important thing on the device.

sections.title: Critical operations power systems (COPS)
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 708 covers power systems for facilities an AHJ or governmental authority has designated as critical operations areas — places like certain 911 and emergency operations centers, critical infrastructure and national-security functions, where losing power is a public-safety event, not an inconvenience. The article layers extra reliability, testing, documentation and risk-assessment duties on top of the standby ideas in Articles 700 to 702.
• The designation comes from the authority — never from the owner, the engineer, or the size of the generator.
• A documented risk assessment (708.4) comes first, and it drives the design, the physical security, and the source choices.
• The alternate source has to carry the designated area at full load for at least 72 hours (708.22(C)).
Sharma's residential and light-commercial work will rarely be designated COPS, and the practical skill is recognizing the designation on the rare job that carries it.
sections.on_the_job: A county emergency operations center in Central Florida asks Sharma to bid a generator replacement, and the front-end documents call the building a designated critical operations area. That one phrase changes the job. Before pricing, confirm the designation in writing and ask for the facility's risk assessment — it sets the physical security, the protection, and the 72-hour full-load run the alternate source has to prove. Price the documented testing and maintenance program as part of the work, not as a favor afterward. And if the designation is not in the documents, say so in the bid: a big generator alone does not make a job a 708 job.

Article 708 exists so the facilities a community leans on hardest are designed against a written list of hazards instead of hope. The risk assessment comes first because the right generator, fuel supply, and protection all depend on what can actually go wrong at that site.

Article 708 applies only where an AHJ or governmental authority has designated the facility or an area in it as critical operations. A warehouse with a big standby set is still an Article 702 job unless somebody with that authority designated it.

sections.title: Stand-Alone systems — power with no utility to lean on
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 710 covers systems that operate in island mode — not connected to a power production and distribution network. The off-grid house, the remote pump, the microgrid that runs alone: if there is no utility behind the source, this article owns the job.
• The supply may be smaller than a normal Article 220 calculated load — but never smaller than the floor 710.15 sets: the combined sources must at least carry the largest single piece of utilization equipment.
• Sources combine freely here: solar, storage and a generator can all feed the same stand-alone system.
• The sources still have to be identified: 710.10 requires a permanent plaque or directory naming each source and its disconnect.
The same equipment often also appears under Articles 702, 705 and 706 when it works alongside a utility, so the first job on any of these systems is deciding which mode it is actually in.
sections.on_the_job: Grove pump house outside Ocala with no utility service available and none coming. Solar array, a battery inverter and a small generator feed one panel — no utility feed exists, so the job is Article 710 from the first sketch, not 702. The load list starts with the well pump, the largest single load on the place. Combined source capacity has to clear that pump load under 710.15, and the 710.10 plaque at the disconnect names all three sources so the next person can shut the system down.
sections.why_it_exists: A utility-fed system borrows the grid's capacity and the grid's fault current. An island system has neither. If the combined sources cannot carry the biggest load the building will ever switch on, the system fails on an ordinary day, not in an emergency — and with no utility to fall back on, a dark off-grid house or a dead well pump is the whole story. The mode decision matters because the wrong article sizes the system by the wrong rule.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is Article 702, picked because the system has a generator. A generator alone does not make it optional standby. Article 702 needs a utility service for the generator to stand by for. With no utility connection at all, the system is stand-alone and Article 710 governs — and 710 sizes the supply by its own floor, not by the standby rules.

sections.title: Identification of power sources — stand-alone systems
sections.plain_explanation:
New in the 2020 code, 710.10 requires the power sources of a stand-alone system to be identified by a permanent plaque or directory. It is the same instinct as the 705.10 directory for interconnected sources: anyone working on or responding to the building can find every source and its disconnect.
• The plaque or directory is installed at the disconnecting means location, or another approved, readily visible location.
• It denotes the location of each power source disconnecting means serving the building.
• Where more than one source supplies the building, the marking carries the multiple-sources caution, the same as 705.10.
• A diagram on the plaque must be oriented the way the building actually sits.
On a system with solar, batteries and a generator scattered around a property, the identification is the difference between a safe shutdown and a scavenger hunt.
sections.on_the_job: On an off-grid house outside Ocala, the plaque at the house disconnect lists all three sources: the PV inverter disconnect and the battery disconnect on the garage west wall, and the generator disconnect in the detached shed. List every source on the identification, including the small generator that 'only feeds the barn.' If it can energize the wiring, it belongs on the list. Walk the property and verify each location before the plaque is made — a directory that points to where a disconnect was planned, instead of where it is, fails its only job.

sections.why_it_exists: A stand-alone system has no utility to call and no single service main to pull. Open the wrong disconnect and the building is still live from the battery inverter in the garage. The plaque is how a firefighter, a responder, or the next electrician finds every source before anyone touches the wiring.
inspection_fails: No plaque at all on an off-grid house — the inspector has to hunt for the battery and generator disconnects.
Plaque lists the PV and the battery but leaves off the generator in the detached shed.
Directory diagram drawn rotated from how the building actually sits, so the responder is sent to the wrong wall.
Hand-lettered paper label taped inside the panel instead of a permanent plaque (110.21(B)).
sections.exam_trap: The system is off-grid, so there is no service equipment, no utility — and, the trap answer says, no directory. Wrong. Section 710.10 was added in 2020 precisely for stand-alone systems, and it asks for the same thing 705.10 asks of interconnected systems. The second trap is citing 705.10 on a stand-alone job: the requirement is real, but on a 710 system it lives in 710.10.

sections.title: General rules — sizing a stand-alone supply
sections.plain_explanation:
Premises wiring fed by a stand-alone system still has to meet the code the way a feeder- or service-fed installation does, with the modifications on this page.
• The supply may be smaller than the Article 220 calculated load. Article 710 does not make an island system pretend the utility is behind it.
• The floor: the combined capacity of all the stand-alone sources must at least equal the load of the largest single piece of utilization equipment connected.
• General lighting load does not count as that single load — the floor is set by real equipment, not by the lighting calc.
• The 2020 code expressly permits these systems to supply three-phase, three-wire or four-wire loads.
sections.on_the_job: Off-grid house in Marion County. The Article 220 worksheet says 12,000 VA, but nobody has to build a 12,000 VA island. The load list is built around the well pump at 3,000 VA — the largest single piece of utilization equipment. A 4,500 VA inverter plus a 3,000 VA generator gives 7,500 VA of combined capacity, comfortably over the pump and well under the 220 number. The lighting load, 1,500 VA, never enters the floor test. What does get checked with the inverter maker is the pump's starting surge, because carrying the running load and starting it are two different days.
sections.why_it_exists: The largest single load is the one demand the system cannot dodge: sooner or later that pump, compressor or range runs by itself, and the sources either carry it or the inverter trips and the building goes dark. Sizing to an average or a diversified number works only while the grid absorbs the peaks — an island has nothing to absorb peaks with. The floor keeps a small system honest without forcing it to be a utility.
sections.exam_trap: The wrong answer treats the general lighting load as the largest single load and sizes the sources to it — 1,500 VA on the diagram's house. Section 710.15 takes lighting out of that test by name. The floor is the largest single piece of utilization equipment, the well pump at 3,000 VA, and a system sized to the lights fails the section's own test the first time the pump starts.

sections.title: Direct-current microgrids
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 712, confirmed in the printed 2020 table of contents, covers dc microgrids: systems that distribute dc power from dc sources to dc loads, with converters tying them to ac systems where needed. It is a young article for a young technology, and Sharma's Florida work has not hit one yet. It earns its place in this book so the reader recognizes the article number and does not mistake a dc microgrid for an Article 710 stand-alone system or a 705 interconnection, which it can sit alongside.
• A dc microgrid is one or more interconnected dc sources, dc-dc converters and dc loads on a common dc bus; ac loads are fed through dc-ac inverters, and the grid ties to the ac system through an ac-dc converter or a bidirectional inverter.
• Dc loads are the point: LED lighting, communications gear, computers and servers, variable-speed drives and HVAC equipment can all run straight off the bus.
• 712.10 wants a directory: a plaque or directory at each service equipment location naming every dc source, and directories at the interconnectable source locations as well.
sections.on_the_job: If a plan set shows a dc bus feeding loads, find this article before you assume the familiar ac rules answer everything. On the first one Sharma lands — most likely a commercial job with LED lighting and a battery-backed server room — the field habit to build early is the directory: at the service equipment, a plaque naming the service and every dc source on the bus, the same discipline 705.10 and 690.56(B) already drill into us on the ac side. No directory, no way for the next crew to know the bus has three parents.

No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: Dc sources do not behave like a utility feed. A battery or PV array on a dc bus can keep that bus energized from several directions at once, and dc arcs do not self-extinguish the way ac arcs do at the zero crossing. An electrician who walks up expecting Article 705 or 710 rules — or plain ac habits — can open the wrong thing in the wrong order. The article exists so the system is recognized, directed and labeled as its own animal.
inspection_fails: Dc bus treated like an ac panel: no directory at the service equipment naming the dc sources (712.10).
System permitted and wired as a 710 stand-alone job when the drawings show a common dc bus — wrong article, wrong rules.
Ac loads tapped straight off the dc bus instead of through a dc-ac inverter.
Second dc source added to the bus with the directory never updated.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: calling it a stand-alone system under Article 710 because it can run without the utility, or wiring it under 705 because sources interconnect. A system built around a common dc bus with dc sources and dc loads is a dc microgrid — Article 712 owns it, whichever articles it sits alongside.

sections.title: Directory — dc microgrid sources
sections.plain_explanation:
712.10 is Article 712's directory rule, the dc counterpart of 705.10 and 710.10:
• A permanent plaque or directory denoting all electric power sources on or in the premises.
• Installed at each service equipment location, and at the locations of power production sources capable of being interconnected.
• Subsection (B) covers the directory for a building supplied by a dc microgrid.
Anyone working the building should be able to find every source and its disconnect from the directory. Other articles send dc microgrid work here for its plaques and directories: battery systems under 480.7(G)(1), PV under 690.56(B), fuel cells under 692.4(B)(2) and wind systems under 694.54(B).
sections.on_the_job: Sharma has not installed a dc microgrid; this page is the signpost for the day one appears on a plan set. When it does — say a small Orlando warehouse with rooftop PV and a battery rack feeding a dc bus for LED lighting — the directory work is roughed and priced like 705.10 work: a permanent directory at the service equipment naming every source, directories at each source that can interconnect, and the disconnect location for each one shown. The field habit transfers directly: directory at the service, every source named, disconnect locations shown.

sections.why_it_exists: A dc microgrid hides its sources in plain sight: a battery rack in a closet, a PV combiner on the roof, a fuel cell by the pad. Open the service and the dc bus can still be live from three directions at once. The directory is how the next electrician — or a firefighter at 2 a.m. — learns that the building has more than one way to be energized, and where each disconnect is.

Directory names the PV array but leaves the battery system off the plaque.

The other wrong turn is citing 705.10 or 710.10: those are the ac counterparts. The dc microgrid directory rule is 712.10, and subsection (B) is the part written for a building supplied by a dc microgrid.

sections.title: Circuits and equipment operating at less than 50 volts
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 720 is the small general article for circuits and equipment running under 50 volts, ac or dc, that are not claimed by a more specific article (720.1, 720.2). Most low-voltage work Sharma does is claimed: thermostats and controls by Article 725, fire alarm by 760, communications by Chapter 8. Article 720 is what remains — and what remains still has teeth:
• Conductors not smaller than 12 AWG copper or equivalent; on an appliance branch circuit supplying more than one appliance or appliance receptacle, not smaller than 10 AWG (720.4).
• Standard lampholders rated not less than 660 W (720.5), and receptacles rated not less than 15 A (720.6).
• Receptacles of not less than 20 A in kitchens, laundries, and other locations where portable appliances are likely to be used (720.7).
• Storage batteries follow the Article 480 rules named in 720.9, and the work is installed in a neat and workmanlike manner, cables supported so normal building use will not damage them (720.11).
sections.on_the_job: Name the owning article for every low-voltage run on the plan. On a shop remodel in Apopka, the crew found a legacy 32 V appliance circuit feeding three receptacles in a detached workshop. No specific article claims it, so Article 720 does: the run is rewired in 10 AWG copper — an appliance branch circuit with more than one receptacle — the receptacles are rated 15 A minimum, and 20 A receptacles go in at the bench where portable tools plug in. 'Low voltage' is a description, not a wiring method.

nec2023_change.change: Article 720 was deleted in the 2023 NEC — the Code panel found the equipment it covered had not been manufactured for decades and no known systems remain in service. Low-voltage work is governed by the specific articles that claim each circuit instead.

sections.title: Article 722 — not in the 2020 code (a 2023 number)
sections.plain_explanation:
There is no Article 722 in NEC 2020. The number was first used in the 2023 edition, where a new Article 722 gathers the cable rules for power-limited circuits that the 2020 book spreads across Articles 725, 760 and 770. Florida work under the Florida Building Code 8th Edition (permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026) is NEC 2020, so a 2023 study book, app or exam sheet that sends you to 722 is pointing at a page this code does not have. In the 2020 book, the cable types, listing and substitution rules for Class 2 and Class 3 circuits live inside Article 725, the power-limited fire alarm cable rules live inside Article 760, and the optical fiber cable rules live in Article 770.

sections.title: Class 1, Class 2 and Class 3 circuits — controls and signaling
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 725 sorts remote-control, signaling and power-limited circuits into three classes, and the class comes from the power source, not from the wire in your hand.
• Class 1 circuits are not power-limited. They can carry serious energy — remote-control and signaling circuits can run up to 600 V — and they are wired much like power circuits.
• Class 2 circuits are limited so strictly at the source that they are treated as safe from both shock and fire initiation: the thermostat, the doorbell, most controls.
• Class 3 circuits allow more voltage and power than Class 2. They stay limited against fire initiation, but the energy can still present a shock hazard, so added protection against shock is part of the deal.
The relaxed wiring methods in this article are earned by the listed power source. Change the source and you may have changed the class — and every wiring rule that came with it.
sections.on_the_job: On every controls job, find the power source and read its label before you choose a cable. No listed Class 2 source, no Class 2 wiring methods. In a Marion Oaks spec house, the air handler's control transformer feeds the thermostat and the condensate float switch: a Class 2 circuit, run in Class 2 cable with no raceway, exactly what the article allows. The 120 V smoke-alarm interconnect on the same plan is not a 725 circuit at all — it is ordinary branch-circuit wiring. Sorting those two at rough-in, by source, is the whole game.

sections.title: Definitions — what makes a circuit Class 2 or Class 3
sections.plain_explanation:
The definitions draw the line this whole article stands on.
• A Class 2 circuit is the wiring between a Class 2 power source and its equipment, with power limited tightly enough that the circuit is considered safe against both electric shock and starting a fire.
• A Class 3 circuit is limited against fire initiation, but its voltage and power can still present a shock hazard, so added protection is part of the deal.
• A Class 1 circuit is everything in this family that is not power-limited that way, including remote-control and signaling circuits that can run up to 600 volts.
The class is a property of the source and the circuit together — never of the cable alone.
sections.on_the_job: When a helper asks why two identical-looking cables get treated differently, the answer is on the source label, and this definition is why. On a Sharma service call, the thermostat run back to a listed Class 2 transformer is Class 2 work; the line-voltage control run beside it is not, even where both are the same gauge and the same color. The lead's rule for the crew: name the class out loud from the source before anyone picks a cable or a box.

Class 2 power is limited so tightly that the wiring can be treated as harmless in places where power wiring could never go. Class 3 trades a little of that safety for more working power, so the code asks for added protection against the shock hazard that remains. Get the definition wrong and every wiring-method decision that follows is built on sand.

sections.title: Power sources for Class 2 and Class 3 circuits
sections.plain_explanation:
A Class 2 or Class 3 circuit has to be fed from a source this section recognizes:
• A listed Class 2 or Class 3 transformer
• A listed Class 2 or Class 3 power supply
• Other listed equipment marked to identify it as the Class 2 or Class 3 source
• One of the other sources the section names, such as certain dry-cell battery supplies
A random wall-wart or an unmarked transformer does not create a Class 2 circuit, however small its output looks. The listing and the marking are the circuit's papers — they are what makes the limited-power wiring methods of Article 725 legal on that run.
sections.on_the_job: On a Winter Park office controls job, Sharma's crew lands a thermostat and zone-control retrofit fed from a listed Class 2 transformer at the air handler. The lead photographs the source label — listing mark, Class 2 marking, output rating — for the job record before the ceiling closes. At final inspection, that photo is the fastest proof of what class the circuit is. When the controls sub ships a panel with an unmarked generic supply instead, it gets swapped for the listed one on the submittal, not in the ceiling.

That promise lives in the listed source, not in the wire. Swap in an unlisted supply with a fault inside it, and the same thin cable can carry far more energy than the method was ever judged for.

sections.title: Wiring methods on the load side of the source
sections.plain_explanation:
On the load side of a Class 2 or Class 3 source, the wiring methods relax. The listed cable types for these circuits — the CL2 and CL3 families, power-limited tray cable and their permitted substitutions — may be installed without the raceways and boxes ordinary power wiring needs, following the application rules for the cable chosen.
• The line is at the source: the supply side is wired under the normal chapters; only the limited-energy side earns the relaxed methods.
• The relaxation is earned by the source — a listed Class 2 or Class 3 source under 725.121 is what makes the circuit Class 2 or Class 3 at all.
• Cable choice still follows the building space it runs through, the way plenum and riser choices do elsewhere in the book: match the cable tier to the space, per 725.154.
sections.on_the_job: Controls rough-in on a small commercial job in Winter Haven. The 120 V feed to the listed Class 2 transformer is run in EMT with boxes, like any other power wiring — that side is Chapter 3 work. From the transformer's load side, the thermostat and damper runs leave in CL2 cable, stapled and supported without raceway, exactly what 725.130 permits. Where one run crosses the return-air ceiling, the cable changes to CL2P for that space. The apprentice's shortcut — CL2 methods all the way back to the panel — is the write-up this page exists to prevent.
sections.why_it_exists: The relaxed methods are safe for one reason: the listed source cannot deliver enough energy to start a fire or give a dangerous shock, so the cable does not need a raceway's protection. That bargain ends at the source's input terminals. Wire the supply side with load-side methods and full branch-circuit energy is riding in an unprotected cable. The tier rules carry the second half of the bargain — the wrong cable in a plenum or a riser shaft spreads smoke and fire between floors.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer extends the relaxed methods to the whole run: 'It is a Class 2 circuit, so Class 2 methods apply from the panel out.' They do not. The relaxation starts on the load side of the listed source. Everything ahead of the source — the 120 V feed that powers it — is wired under the normal chapters, raceways and boxes included.

sections.title: Separation from power conductors — the general rule
sections.plain_explanation:
725.136 is the separation rule for limited-energy control wiring. Class 2 and Class 3 cables and conductors may not be placed in the same cable, raceway, enclosure, box or similar fitting as any of these:
• Electric light and power conductors
• Class 1 conductors
• Non-power-limited fire alarm conductors
• Medium-power network-powered broadband conductors
unless one of the permissions in this section applies. The standing permissions are:
• Separation by a barrier inside the shared enclosure, raceway or fitting
• The tight rules for conductors that enter the same equipment, where the two families have to meet
• The spacing rule for other applications, covered on the next page at 725.136(I)
The 2 in figure inside this section is real, but it belongs to that one paragraph — the open-run spacing rule. It is not a general clearance for every low-voltage run, and it never licenses sharing a box.
sections.on_the_job: On a Marion Oaks spec house, the air handler's control leads are Class 2: the thermostat run and the condensate float-switch leads. The 240 V power whip lands in the air handler's disconnect and its own compartment; the Class 2 leads enter through their own opening and stay out of the power side, meeting the equipment only where the equipment rules allow it. In the attic, the Class 2 run and the air handler's power cable travel the same direction for about 20 ft. Keep the two runs at least 2 in apart for that stretch, or put one side in a raceway — the 2 in rule covers open runs like this one. It does not carry into the junction box at the end of the run; in the box, the barrier and equipment permissions govern.

Put that cable in the same box as a 120 V conductor and one fault, one nicked jacket or one careless splice can put line voltage on a cable that runs through the whole building, gets handled like bell wire, and lands on equipment never built for it. Separation keeps the limited-energy system limited in fact, not just at the source.

sections.title: Other applications — the 2-inch spacing rule
sections.plain_explanation:
For applications outside enclosures and equipment, Class 2 and Class 3 conductors are separated by at least 2 inches from conductors of electric light, power, Class 1, non-power-limited fire alarm and medium-power broadband circuits — unless one of the exceptions does the separating instead:
• One side or the other is in a raceway, or in a metal-sheathed, metal-clad, nonmetallic-sheathed or Type UF cable.
• The two are permanently separated by a suitable insulating barrier or tubing.
The parallel rule for communications circuits lives in Chapter 8 at 800.133(A)(2), and it is also 2 inches, with its own raceway and cable exceptions. Two inches is a spacing for open runs, not a license to share a box, and not a number to apply where a barrier rule already governs.
sections.on_the_job: Attic of a Marion Oaks spec house: the Class 2 thermostat and alarm runs cross the same joist bays as the NM power runs. Because the power side is nonmetallic-sheathed cable, the exception covers those crossings with no open-air spacing to hold. Where a Class 2 run leaves the cable's protection and runs open beside the air handler's power conductors, the crew holds the full 2 inches along the run — and carries the exceptions with the number, not instead of it.
sections.why_it_exists: Class 2 and Class 3 wiring is built and insulated for low energy. Run it tight against power conductors and a power fault — or even steady induced voltage — lands on thermostat, data and signaling cable that was never made to carry it. Two inches of air, or a raceway, cable sheath or barrier doing the same job, keeps the fault on the side that can take it.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is using the 2-inch rule inside a box. 725.136(I) covers applications outside enclosures and equipment; sharing an enclosure is a different paragraph with barrier rules of its own. The reverse trap also fails answers: the 2 inches is not absolute — a raceway, a sheathed cable on either side, or a permanent barrier satisfies the section without it.

sections.title: Power and data in the same cable — 725.144 and PoE heating
sections.plain_explanation:
When a Class 2 cable carries power and data together — Power over Ethernet feeding cameras, access points, and lighting — every powered pair adds heat to the bundle, and a big bundle of powered cables runs hotter than the same bundle carrying data alone. 725.144 answers with ampacity limits for the conductors of Class 2 cables used to transmit power: the permitted current depends on the conductor size, the cable's temperature rating, and how many cables are bundled together. Type LP (limited power) cables carry their permitted ampacity in the cable marking, which takes the bundle question out of the table and puts it on the jacket. A cable that is fine for data is not automatically fine as a power-delivery cable in a full bundle.

sections.title: Instrumentation tray cable — Type ITC
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 727 covers instrumentation tray cable — Type ITC — a factory assembly of insulated conductors in a flame-retardant jacket, used for instrumentation and control circuits run in tray, largely in industrial work.
• Sharma's residential and light-commercial crews will meet it rarely, if ever.
• The article sits between 725 and 728 in the printed book, and the reader should know what the cable is when a commercial plan calls it out.
• ITC is not a substitute for a Class 2 cable job, and its permitted uses follow its own article — a plan that specifies ITC gets ITC.
sections.on_the_job: A small water-treatment control building outside Ocala is light-commercial work, but the spec calls out Type ITC in tray for the instrument loops between the control panel and the field sensors. Sharma prices and orders ITC as its own wiring method, run in tray under Article 727. The value-engineering suggestion to run thermostat wire instead is rejected at the estimate: different cable, different article, different permitted uses. If a plan specifies ITC, it is priced and ordered as its own wiring method — not value-engineered into thermostat wire.

sections.title: Fire-resistive cable systems
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 728 covers fire-resistive cable systems: listed systems, cable included, that are built and installed to keep critical circuits working through a rated period of fire exposure. These are the systems behind circuit-integrity cable on life-safety feeders — emergency feeders, fire pump feeders and critical operations circuits.
• The listing is a system, not just a cable. A system listed to UL 2196 (an FHIT system in the UL Fire Resistance Directory) names the exact cable, raceway, supports, splice kits and boxes, and the spacing of the supports.
• Install it exactly as the system listing describes, supports and all. A field substitution breaks the rating even when the cable itself looks identical.
• Where Article 728 and another article of the Code differ, Article 728 applies (728.3). The listing instructions are part of the installation, not paperwork.
• Listed systems carry a rated period — commonly 1 hour or 2 hours. The circuit being protected sets which rating the job needs.
sections.on_the_job: A 12-story condo on the Orlando corridor stands over 75 ft tall, so 700.10(D) requires 2-hour fire protection for its emergency feeders. Sharma runs the life-safety feeder as one listed 2-hour circuit-integrity system: cable, raceway, supports and splice kits all come from the single FHIT system on the approved submittal, and supports go at the spacing that system prints — not the spacing the crew usually uses. Photograph supports and terminations as you go; the rating lives in those details, and the inspector can ask for the FHIT document by number.

sections.why_it_exists: A fire does not wait for the panel schedule. The emergency feeder runs the exit lights, the fire alarm, the smoke control fans and the fire pump while people are still inside the building, and ordinary cable fails within minutes under direct flame. A fire-resistive system buys the rated time — up to 2 hours — for everyone to get out and for firefighters to work.

The same cable installed any other way is an unrated installation wearing a rated cable.

sections.title: Energy management systems
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 750 covers energy management systems: equipment that monitors and controls how a building uses energy, including the load-management systems that Articles 702 and 705 lean on when a generator or a panel is deliberately run below its unmanaged peak. The article's guardrail is that managing energy never means defeating safety: controls may shed, schedule and limit loads within their listings, and the overcurrent and disconnect rules of the rest of the book still stand behind them.
In the 2020 book the article itself is short, and the places an EMS earns its keep are specific. Automatic load management lets an optional standby source be sized to the maximum load the management system will actually connect (702.4(B)(2)), and a power control system under 705.13 can limit how much current an interconnected source puts on a busbar. Both methods stand or fall on the settings staying where they were set.
sections.on_the_job: A Marion Oaks house with a 200 A service adds a whole-house standby generator on an automatic transfer switch. The load the switch would transfer is more than the 22 kW generator — about 92 A at 240 V — can carry, so Sharma installs listed load management: the range, the electric water heater and the 5-ton air conditioner are shed in a set priority order, and the generator is sized to the maximum load the management system will actually connect, the load-management duty in 702.4(B)(2). The settings are recorded in the job file, the managed circuits are marked at the panel, and the system is proven by running the house on generator power before the job closes.

The EMS gets one current setpoint: the load used in the 220.70 calculation and the most current it allows on the supply it controls (750.30(C)(1)).

The guardrail exists because an EMS is a control, not a protective device — when it fails, or someone changes it, the overcurrent protection behind it is the last line of defense.

sections.title: Fire alarm systems — wiring and power
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 760 covers the installation of wiring and equipment for fire alarm systems, including the circuits the fire alarm system controls and powers: detection, notification, sprinkler waterflow and supervisory signals, and functions like door release and elevator control that the alarm commands. System design, device placement and testing live in NFPA 72; this article governs how the wiring and power are installed.
Every fire alarm circuit is one of two kinds, and the kind comes from its power source, exactly the way Article 725 classes come from theirs:
• Non-power-limited (NPLFA) — fed under 760.41, wired like power circuits
• Power-limited (PLFA) — fed from a listed PLFA source under 760.121
sections.on_the_job: First question on alarm work: which circuits are NPLFA and which are PLFA? The answer picks the cable, the wiring method and the separation rules for every run. On a small Orlando medical-office build-out, Sharma's crew starts at the panel: the branch circuit feeding the FACP is dedicated to the fire alarm, its disconnect is identified in red and marked FIRE ALARM CIRCUIT, and its location is identified at the control unit (760.41(B) / 760.121(B)). The initiating loop and the notification circuits take their kind from the panel's listed source, and the crew labels each run before the ceiling closes — the next electrician should never have to guess which kind he is opening.

sections.why_it_exists: A fire alarm has to work on the worst day of the building's life, while other systems are failing around it. Mixing up the two circuit kinds — or feeding the panel from a borrowed branch circuit — can leave the system dead, unsupervised, or damaged by a fault it was never built to ride through. The article's split at the power source is what keeps alarm wiring from being treated like bell wire.
inspection_fails: FACP fed from a shared branch circuit that also carries receptacles or lights — the fire alarm branch circuit feeds nothing else.
Fire alarm disconnect with no red identification and no FIRE ALARM CIRCUIT marking.
PLFA cable and methods used on a circuit whose source is not a listed PLFA source.
Alarm branch circuit run through GFCI or AFCI protection, which 760.41(B) and 760.121(B) do not allow.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that Article 760 designs the fire alarm system — device spacing, coverage, and testing. It does not. Design, placement and testing live in NFPA 72; Article 760 governs how the wiring and power are installed. Second trap: calling a circuit power-limited because the cable jacket says PLFA. The kind comes from the power source, not the cable.

sections.title: Fire alarm circuit identification
sections.plain_explanation:
Fire alarm circuits are identified at terminal and junction locations, in a manner that helps prevent unintentional signals on the fire alarm circuits during testing and servicing of other systems.
• The identification lives where the work happens: at the terminals and at every junction location, not just on a panel schedule in the office.
• Alarm wiring that nobody can tell apart from everything else in a ceiling is an invitation to the next trade to disturb it.
• The manner of identification has to do its job — it must actually keep other work from putting false signals on the alarm circuits.
sections.on_the_job: On a tenant build-out in Altamonte Springs, the alarm circuits run through the same ceiling as the lighting and the HVAC controls. Identify as you terminate: every fire alarm circuit tagged at the panel terminals, and again at each junction box a later electrician might open — the box above the corridor, the splice over the stockroom. When the controls contractor comes back to test his system, he can see at a glance which conductors are not his. The identification is part of the install, not paperwork for the end of the job.

sections.why_it_exists: Fire alarm circuits share ceilings and junction boxes with power, lighting and low-voltage wiring. When a technician testing another system cannot tell which conductors are the alarm loop, a lifted lead or a stray jumper can put a false signal on the system — or silently take a detection circuit out of service. Identification at the points where hands actually touch the wiring is what keeps other work from becoming an alarm event.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer identifies the circuits only at the fire alarm control panel, or only on the drawings. 760.30 puts the identification at terminal and junction locations — the places where testing and service work actually opens the wiring. A panel schedule in the office does not stop a false signal in the ceiling.

sections.title: Circuit requirements — NPLFA follows Parts I and II, PLFA follows Parts I and III
sections.plain_explanation:
This short section is the traffic cop of Article 760: it tells you which parts of the article govern a circuit before you read any other rule.
• Non-power-limited fire alarm (NPLFA) circuits comply with Part I (general) and Part II (non-power-limited circuits).
• Power-limited fire alarm (PLFA) circuits comply with Part I (general) and Part III (power-limited circuits).
The circuit's family comes from its power source — 760.41 for NPLFA, 760.121 for PLFA — not from the wire on the truck. The two families allow different cables, different overcurrent protection, and different installation methods, so a rule read from the wrong part is a rule that does not apply: the classic Article 760 error.
sections.on_the_job: On a Winter Garden warehouse job, the drawings showed one fire alarm control unit fed from a dedicated branch circuit — an NPLFA system — and a second, smaller panel whose listed supply made its circuits power-limited. The apprentice priced one cable type for both. The foreman split the order: Parts I and II for the first system, Parts I and III for the second. Different cable, different protection, different separation rules — all of it decided by 760.35 before a single reel was cut.
sections.why_it_exists: The two families carry very different energy. An NPLFA circuit is fed like a power circuit and can deliver fault energy that starts fires; a PLFA source is limited, so its circuits cannot. Rules written for one energy level are wrong for the other: too lax for NPLFA, needlessly strict for PLFA. 760.35 exists so the installer sorts the circuit first and only then opens the rulebook.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer sends both families to the same parts — usually 'Part I and Part II for everything,' because Part II comes first in the article. PLFA circuits are governed by Parts I and III. If a question names a power-limited fire alarm circuit and an answer choice cites a Part II rule, it is wrong no matter how good the rule sounds.

sections.title: NPLFA circuit power source requirements
sections.plain_explanation: A non-power-limited fire alarm circuit is powered from a source that follows the normal wiring chapters, with output voltage not over 600 volts nominal. The branch circuit feeding the fire alarm equipment feeds nothing else, and the fire alarm circuit disconnect is allowed to be secured in the on position so a casual hand cannot silence the system's power. Section 760.41(B) adds the identification package: the overcurrent device is identified at the fire alarm control unit, the disconnecting means carries red identification marked FIRE ALARM CIRCUIT and is accessible only to qualified personnel, and the branch circuit is not supplied through ground-fault or arc-fault circuit-interrupter protection. NPLFA circuits carry real energy, which is why their conductors and protection are handled on the next pages like power wiring, not like bell wire.
sections.on_the_job: Dedicate the branch circuit and label it. If another load wants that circuit later, the answer is no, and this section is the reason you give.

sections.title: NPLFA overcurrent protection — small conductors, small limits
sections.plain_explanation:
Overcurrent protection for non-power-limited fire alarm (NPLFA) circuits is sized off the conductor, and the small conductors alarm work runs on get hard caps:
• 18 AWG conductors: overcurrent protection not over 7 A.
• 16 AWG conductors: overcurrent protection not over 10 A.
• Conductors 14 AWG and larger: protected in accordance with their ampacity.
The device is located where the conductor receives its supply, the way overcurrent protection normally works. Size the device to the smallest conductor on the run: a circuit that leaves the supply on 14 AWG and finishes on 18 AWG is protected as an 18 AWG circuit.
sections.on_the_job: On a strip-center fire alarm retrofit in Kissimmee, the notification runs leaving the power supplies were pulled in 18 AWG and 16 AWG, and the panel schedule showed the shop's standard 20 A breaker out of habit. The foreman caught it before trim: the 18 AWG legs went on protection not over 7 A and the 16 AWG legs not over 10 A, with each device at the point where its conductor receives supply, sized to the smallest conductor on the run, exactly as 760.43 requires.
sections.why_it_exists: A fault on an 18 AWG alarm conductor behind a 20 A breaker can cook the conductor's insulation long before the breaker notices: the wire becomes the fuse. Fire alarm circuits are also the last circuits that may ever fail silently, because a burned-open initiating circuit leaves a building with no alarm and no warning. Capping the protection at 7 A and 10 A keeps the small conductors from being the weak link in a life-safety system.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer sizes the device to the load: 'the horns only draw a few amps, so a 20 A breaker is fine.' 760.43 caps the device by conductor size, not by load: 7 A maximum on 18 AWG and 10 A maximum on 16 AWG, no matter how small the connected load is. When the question is about a fire alarm circuit, answer from Article 760, not from general breaker habit.

sections.title: Power sources for PLFA circuits — and the red breaker
sections.plain_explanation: A power-limited fire alarm circuit is fed from a listed PLFA transformer, a listed PLFA power supply, or listed equipment marked to identify its PLFA source — a fire alarm control panel with an integral source is the everyday example. The branch circuit behind that source feeds no other loads, its overcurrent device is identified in red, is accessible only to qualified personnel, and is marked as the fire alarm circuit, with the device identified at the fire alarm control unit. The red breaker is how the next electrician, and the building's own staff, learn in one glance which breaker must never be casually borrowed or switched. 760.121(B) imposes the same supply package as the non-power-limited rule in 760.41(B): the branch-circuit disconnecting means is identified in red and marked “FIRE ALARM CIRCUIT,” its location is identified at the fire alarm control unit, access is limited to qualified personnel — and the branch circuit must not be supplied through a ground-fault circuit-interrupter or arc-fault circuit-interrupter protective device.
sections.on_the_job: Use the red identification and the panel marking on every alarm job, and verify the branch circuit truly serves nothing else before you sign the panel schedule.

sections.title: Installation of PLFA cables in buildings
sections.plain_explanation:
Power-limited fire alarm cables are installed by application: this section, working with the cable application and substitution tables later in the article, matches each listed cable type to where it may run — plenums, risers, trays, raceways and general building spaces. The method is table-driven on purpose: the cable's fire listing, not its color or its price, decides where it belongs. Circuit-integrity cable appears in this family where a design calls for circuits that must survive fire exposure, and it is installed as its listing directs.
• Fabricated ducts for environmental air follow 300.22(B) — the cable runs in a raceway (760.135(B)).
• Plenums and other environmental-air spaces: FPLP only (760.135(C), with 300.22(C)).
• Riser runs: FPLP or FPLR (760.135(D)); in a metal raceway with firestops at each floor, FPL may also run (760.135(E)).
• Fireproof shafts: all three types (760.135(F)); one- and two-family dwellings: all three (760.135(G)); other locations: all three (760.135(H)).
• Substitution only runs downhill: FPLP may replace FPLR or FPL, and FPLR may replace FPL — never the reverse (Table 760.154).
• A CI suffix (FPLR-CI, for example) marks circuit-integrity cable, installed as its listing directs.
sections.on_the_job: On an Ocala medical-office fit-out, the ceiling is a return-air plenum, so every fire alarm run above it is FPLP — the red FPL left over from the last job stays on the truck, whatever its color promises. The vertical run to the second floor goes in the shaft as FPLR. The tech reads the jacket legend out loud at the rough-in walk: type first, then the space it is entering, then the table row. That ten-second habit is the whole section in practice.

sections.why_it_exists: Fire alarm cable has to work during the fire, not just before it. A cable whose jacket burns and smokes in a ceiling plenum feeds the very air stream the building breathes, and a riser shaft is a chimney that carries flame floor to floor. Matching the cable's fire listing to the space is how the alarm circuits survive long enough to do their one job — get people out.
inspection_fails: Plain FPL run through a ceiling plenum — the space required FPLP (760.135(C)).
FPL substituted upward for FPLR in a riser shaft; substitution only runs downhill (Table 760.154).
Riser run in a metal raceway with no firestops at the floor penetrations, so the (E) conditions are unmet.
Cable type chosen from the jacket color at the truck instead of the printed legend.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: “the cable is red, so it is fire alarm cable and it can go anywhere.” Color is not a listing. Plain FPL in a ceiling plenum fails 760.135(C) even though it is the right color and the right system — the space demanded FPLP, and only the jacket legend tells you what you are holding.

sections.title: Optical fiber cables
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 770, the last article of Chapter 7, covers installing optical fiber cables — glass or plastic fibers carrying light instead of current. The signal cannot shock anyone or start a fire, so the article spends its force on the cable's fire and smoke listing for the space it runs through, and on what happens when fiber shares raceways and enclosures with conductors that do carry energy.
• Two families. A nonconductive cable (the N types, like OFNP) has no metal in it. A conductive cable (the C types, like OFCP) has a metallic member, armor or sheath — metal that can import a fault or a foreign voltage.
• Listing by space, 770.179 and 770.154: plenum cable (OFNP, OFCP) for ducts and air spaces; riser cable (OFNR, OFCR) for vertical runs; general-purpose cable (OFNG, OFCG, and OFN, OFC) for the rest. A higher-listed cable may substitute for a lower one — never the other way around.
• Sharing space, 770.133: nonconductive fiber may occupy a raceway or tray with light, power and Class 1 conductors, but not a cabinet, box or panel with those circuits' terminations, unless functionally associated with them. Conductive fiber may not share a raceway or tray with light, power or Class 1 circuits. A composite cable — fiber and conductors in one jacket — is permitted only where the two are functionally associated.
• From outside, 770.48: unlisted outside-plant fiber may run up to 50 ft in from its point of entrance, and must end in an enclosure.
Communications fiber also appears in Chapter 8's world; 770 is fiber's home for installation rules.
sections.on_the_job: Office fit-out in Winter Park: the data contractor's reel is marked OFN — general purpose — but the run goes 120 ft across a return-air plenum ceiling and up a two-story shaft. OFN fails both spaces. The fix: OFNP across the plenum, OFNR up the shaft — or OFNP the whole way, since plenum cable substitutes downward. The carrier's unlisted cable comes 30 ft inside to the demarc enclosure — within the 50 ft limit of 770.48, so it stays.
sections.why_it_exists: The light in a fiber is harmless, but the jacket around it burns. A general-purpose cable in a shaft or return-air ceiling carries fire and smoke where the building climbs and breathes. The conductive member is the second hazard: steel or armor that touches something live can carry that voltage into a box of low-voltage terminations, where nobody expects a shock.
sections.exam_trap: The exam's favorite answer is "fiber carries no current, so the cable type does not matter." It does: the listing follows the space, not the signal. The paired trap runs the other way: an OFNR riser cable offered as a substitute for OFNP in a plenum. Substitutions go down the ladder only, never up.
inspection_fails: OFN or OFNG cable run across a return-air plenum ceiling with no plenum listing.
Riser shaft wired with general-purpose cable instead of OFNR or better.
Conductive fiber cable sharing a raceway with 120 V power conductors.
Unlisted outside-plant fiber run 80 ft into the building, past the 50 ft entrance limit.
Nonconductive fiber landed in a panel enclosure with power terminations, with no functional association.

sections.title: Installing optical fiber cables
sections.plain_explanation: 770.133 governs how optical fiber cables are installed with other systems. The dividing line is whether the fiber cable is conductive — carrying a metallic strength member, armor, or sheath — or nonconductive. Nonconductive fiber may share a raceway, enclosure, or cable tray with electric light, power, and Class 1 conductors under the conditions the section sets, because the fiber itself brings no conductive path into the box. Conductive fiber is treated with more suspicion: its metal member can carry a fault or a foreign potential into the enclosure, so the section restricts how it mixes with power conductors. Either way, the fiber cable's own listing for the space (770.179) still applies, and abandoned fiber comes out under the same discipline as the rest of Chapter 7.
sections.on_the_job: Pulling fiber toward a panel-adjacent raceway: the first question is conductive or nonconductive — read the jacket. Nonconductive dielectric fiber is the easy roommate; a steel-armored fiber changes the answer and gets its own path.
sections.figure_idea: Two raceway cross-sections: nonconductive fiber sharing with power; conductive fiber separated.

sections.title: Optical fiber cable types — reading the letters
sections.plain_explanation: The type letters on an optical fiber cable tell you two things: whether the cable is conductive, and where its fire and smoke listing lets it run. OFN is optical fiber nonconductive; OFC is optical fiber conductive — the C means a metallic member is part of the cable. The suffix grades the listing like the communications ladder in Chapter 8: OFNP and OFCP are plenum grade, OFNR and OFCR are riser grade, and plain OFN and OFC are general purpose. A higher grade may substitute for a lower one; a lower grade never substitutes up. Match the letters to the space — plenum, riser, or general — the same way you match CMP, CMR, and CM. OFNG/OFCG and OFN/OFC are general-purpose grade. A nonconductive type may substitute for the conductive type of the same or lower grade (e.g., OFNR for OFCR), but a conductive type never substitutes for a nonconductive one.
sections.on_the_job: Spec says OFNR for a riser shaft and the truck has OFN: that pull does not happen. Plenum-rated fiber (OFNP or OFCP) in the truck covers the riser too — the ladder only runs downhill.
